Title: Autonomous Agentic AI Architectures for Optimizing Security Operations Centers (SOC) KPIs: Methodology, Impact on Detection, Response, and Recovery
Authors: Miroslav Stefanov; Kristyan Stefanov; Laxima Niure Kandel; Sean Crouse (Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University, Daytona Beach, USA); Boyan Jekov (University of Library Science and Information Technology, Sofia, Bulgaria)
Year & Venue: 2025; Land Forces Academy Review, Vol. XXX, No. 3(119), pp. 479-493; DOI 10.2478/raft-2025-0046. Venue is NOT INDEXED in Scopus/SJR (mandatory stratum caveat, PDR-0007).
Core Problem Addressed: SOCs face alert fatigue from the large volume of false-positive alerts that burdens analysts and raises the risk of overlooking genuine threats, delayed responses due to lack of prioritization and fragmented incident management, and insufficient accuracy in event classification that distorts KPI metrics and reduces report reliability (Abstract, p. 479; §1, p. 480). Since KPIs such as TTD, TTR, MTTR, and SIER are the fundamental instrument for assessing SOC detection, response, and recovery maturity (§1, p. 480), the study targets an integrated intelligent system for automated KPI management that adaptively reduces alerts, accelerates response, and improves metric-assessment accuracy (§1, p. 480).
Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: An Agentic AI architecture of ten specialized agents covering the full SOC security/operations lifecycle (§3.3, pp. 483-484): TTD Monitoring Agent (rule-based, no ML; computes timestamp_occurred vs timestamp_detected and alerts on threshold breaches, p. 483); FNR Analysis Agent (XGBoost classifier, recommends mitigation playbooks, p. 483); FPR Suppression Agent (XGBoost plus dynamic suppression; auto-filters alerts with severity < 3 and logs actions in detection_rules.json, p. 483); TTR Response Agent (LightGBM regressor; on detected delays automatically triggers predefined playbook scenarios and notifies teams, pp. 483-484); IRR Tracking Agent (task-closure ratio with automated reminders, p. 483); SIHR Validation Agent (remediation-checklist completeness alerts, pp. 483-484); MTTR Recovery Agent (LightGBM regressor; simulates automated task assignment when thresholds are exceeded, p. 484); OE Task Agent (on-time task proportion with reminders below 30%, p. 484); CSR Feedback Agent (fine-tuned BERT classifying feedback as Positive/Neutral/Negative in real time, p. 484); SIER Metrics Agent (rule-based incidents-to-events ratio with threshold alerts, p. 484). Agents operate as an integrated system with consistent information exchange and shared model/config files (clf_fpr.model, clf_fnr.model, reg_ttr.txt, reg_mttr.txt, detection_rules.json) (§3.3, p. 484). The agentic paradigm is non-LLM: rules plus classical ML (XGBoost, LightGBM, fine-tuned BERT), with no LLM reasoning or orchestration layer.
Methodology: Design-and-demonstration study on real and publicly available data: 214 CSV files (5,270.09 MB; 25,182,806 initial records) cleaned to 8,628,160 observations with 343 unique columns (§3.1, p. 481), consolidated into a unified schema from CICIDS2017, CSE-CIC-IDS2018, CTU-13 Botnet Dataset, Elastic Security Example Datasets, and Wazuh Cloud Demo, emulating SIEM event/alert logs, Incident Management, Task Tracking, and CRM/feedback logs (§3.1, pp. 481-482). Five ML models on three algorithms (Table 1, p. 482; §3.2, pp. 482-483): two XGBoost classifiers (FNR, FPR), two LightGBM regressors (TTR, MTTR) trained offline with periodic monthly retraining (§3.2, p. 483), and a fine-tuned BERT sentiment analyzer for CSR trained 20 epochs on an 80%/20% train/test split (§4.3, pp. 486-487). Evaluation combines internal model metrics (Accuracy/F1/AUC, Table 2, p. 484; MAE/MSE/R², Table 3, p. 486; loss curves, Figure 3, p. 487) with one end-to-end demonstrative execution of the agent workflows on the prepared dataset, reported via console logs and visualizations of computed KPI values and triggered actions (§4.4, pp. 487-491). No comparative baseline, no ablation, and no deployment in a live SOC.
Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: Not specified quantitatively — the paper executes no empirical comparison against a concrete baseline (no before/after measurement and no non-agentic control), so no MTTD/MTTR reduction can be attributed. The abstract's claim of "reduced detection and response times" (Abstract, p. 479) is supported only by (a) internal model-quality metrics — TTR regressor MAE 18%, MSE 1000, R² 0.85; MTTR regressor MAE 20%, MSE 1160, R² 0.80 (Table 3, p. 486) — and (b) KPI readouts from a single demonstrative run: TTD measured at 0.01 seconds against a 3-minute threshold (§4.4.1, p. 488); all 11 processed incidents showed TTR between 655 and 4192 minutes, exceeding the 300-minute threshold and auto-generating warnings (§4.4.2, p. 489); the MTTR model predicted 1884.2 hours, triggering automated task assignment (§4.4.3, p. 490); IRR 85.6% vs 90% threshold and 49 incomplete remediation checklists also triggered alerts (§4.4.2, p. 489). These are outputs of the system itself (internal model values and threshold checks), not measured improvements relative to any baseline SOC process.
General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: Contributes a task-specialized agent-per-KPI design pattern in which each of the ten agents couples one metric to monitoring, prediction, and automated action — playbook triggering, alert suppression, task auto-assignment, reminders, and notifications — with coordinated information exchange across agents (§3.3, pp. 483-484). Demonstrates feasibility of agentic KPI automation over 8.6M+ rows "without the need for manual intervention in most processing phases" (Abstract, p. 479). Reported model performance: FNR classifier Accuracy 80%, F1 0.76, AUC 0.78 outperforms the FPR classifier (Accuracy 65%, F1 0.71, AUC 0.74) (Table 2, p. 484), with jagged ROC curves attributed to smaller or imbalanced test sets (§4.1, p. 485); the BERT model kept Eval Loss stable at ~1.02-1.06 with no overfitting signs (§4.3, pp. 486-487). Claimed advantages are modularity, flexibility, scalability, and reduced team workload and alert-fatigue risk (§5, p. 491). The paper exemplifies the rules-plus-classical-ML (non-LLM) strand of agentic SOC automation, a useful contrast class for LLM-based multi-agent frameworks.
Limitations / Future Work: Authors acknowledge that building the architecture requires substantial initial resources, a high level of expertise, and continuous model maintenance through periodic retraining, and that excessive automation risks insufficient attention to new or unexpected threats falling outside the scope of pre-trained agents (§5, pp. 491-492). Future work: integrating continual learning for adaptation to emerging threats, applying Explainable AI (XAI) to increase transparency and trust in automated decisions, and additional research in real operational environments for more robust validation (§5, p. 492). Implicit limitations evident from the text: single demonstrative execution with no baseline or control (§4.4, pp. 487-491), public/benchmark datasets rather than a live SOC (§3.1, pp. 481-482), and only moderate FPR-classifier performance (Accuracy 65%, Table 2, p. 484).
Relevance to My Thesis: Relevant as architectural evidence for an agent-per-KPI design that directly instruments the thesis's target metric family — detection (TTD/FPR/FNR) and response/recovery (TTR/MTTR) — with autonomous playbook triggering and task auto-assignment (§3.3, pp. 483-484) that resemble copilot actuation in incident response, plus a reusable catalog of 16 indicators in 4 KPI categories (§2, pp. 480-481). However, it provides no causal evidence that an agentic system reduces MTTD/MTTR, since no baseline comparison is executed (§4.4, pp. 487-491). The study enters the corpus with the mandatory stratum caveat — Land Forces Academy Review is NOT INDEXED (NÃO INDEXADO, PDR-0007) — and represents a non-LLM agentic paradigm (rule-based agents plus XGBoost/LightGBM/BERT), contrasting with the LLM-centric copilots central to the thesis; it is best used as a comparison point on the agentic-autonomy spectrum and as KPI-instrumentation groundwork.
Relevance Score: Medium — directly proposes a ten-agent Agentic AI architecture for SOC KPI automation explicitly targeting TTD/TTR/MTTR with automated playbook triggering, but the evidence is a demonstrative execution with internal model metrics only (no empirical baseline comparison), the paradigm is non-LLM (rules + classical ML), and the venue is not indexed (PDR-0007).

Title: From Manual to Agentic Security Operations: A Multi-Dimensional Evaluation of AI-Driven SOC Architectures (title page, p. 1).
Authors: Mutaz Abdel Wahed (Faculty of Information Technology, Jadara University, Irbid, Jordan; corresponding author) and Nader Mohammad Aljawarneh (School of Business, Jadara University, Irbid, Jordan) (p. 1).
Year & Venue: 2026 — Journal of Information & Knowledge Management (World Scientific), Vol. 25, No. 9, art. 2650039 (27 pages), DOI 10.1142/S0219649226500395; received 23 Jan 2026, accepted 1 Mar 2026, published 22 Jun 2026 (p. 1).
Core Problem Addressed: Security Operations Centres (SOCs) face rising alert volumes, analyst overload and fatigue, delayed incident response and inconsistent decision quality, with most alerts being false alarms that still require manual analysis (Abstract, p. 1; §1, p. 2). SOAR-based automation remains reactive, rule/script-driven and dependent on human judgment, so it does not solve the scalability and cognitive limits of analyst-centric SOCs (§1, p. 2; §2, p. 4). In parallel, academic literature lacks a rigorous framework to evaluate the operational impact of autonomous/AI-driven SOCs: existing maturity and benchmarking models focus on tooling and process and ignore decision autonomy, decision quality and analyst experience, and often fail to distinguish scripted automation from true agentic autonomy (§1, pp. 2-3; §2, p. 5).
Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: The paper proposes (i) the 3E multi-dimensional evaluation framework — Efficiency (detection/response latency), Effectiveness (false-positive reduction, remediation success) and Experience (analyst workload and decision oversight) — mapped to RQ1-RQ4 (§3, p. 6; Table 1 and Fig. 2, p. 7), and (ii) an agentic SOC architecture in which AI agents autonomously ingest, enrich, cluster, prioritise and remediate alerts under 'bounded autonomy' with humans kept at strategic checkpoints for high-severity or ambiguous incidents (§3, p. 10; Fig. 3, p. 11; §4, p. 17). The architecture is layered — perception (SIEM/EDR/network telemetry), reasoning (rule-based logic plus probabilistic classifiers), orchestration (autonomous actions, escalation, human-in-the-loop interventions) and execution with a feedback learning loop (§3, p. 10) — and implements a multi-tier remediation hierarchy (Network, Endpoint, Identity, System Integrity controls; Table 6, p. 15). Agentic AI's role is thus autonomous Tier-1 triage/pre-classification and confidence-scored remediation, shifting analysts to supervisory governance (§3, p. 8; §4, pp. 15-16).
Methodology: Comparative operational evaluation (simulation study) contrasting two SOC scenarios — a traditional analyst-centric SIEM/manual-triage workflow versus an agentic AI-enhanced workflow — over a 90-day simulated observation window using synthetic but empirically grounded security telemetry calibrated on SOC benchmarking research and industry surveys (alert frequency, severity distribution, escalation patterns), since production telemetry is sensitive and no public end-to-end datasets exist (§3, pp. 6, 8). Both scenarios share identical alert sources, distributions and observation windows for internal validity (§3, pp. 6, 10). Quantitative metrics are formally defined: MTTD, MTTR, False Positive Ratio, Escalation Rate and Automation Impact (§3, p. 12); analysis uses descriptive statistics and effect-oriented percentage comparisons, explicitly avoiding hypothesis testing for the operational contrast (§3, p. 10). Complementarily, PLS-SEM over 5,571 alert-level observations tests four latent constructs (analyst efficiency, alert complexity, automation impact, decision quality) with composite reliability >0.70 and AVE >0.50 (§3, p. 11; Table 8, p. 20), and a confusion matrix (N=5,571) yields precision 0.873, recall 0.929, F1 0.900, accuracy 0.951 (§4, p. 22; Fig. 10). The Experience dimension uses system-based proxies (intervention frequency, override rates, reassignments) — no direct analyst survey was carried out (§3, pp. 6, 10).
Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: Central metrics, empirically compared against a concrete baseline (the traditional analyst-centric SOC workflow) — but both arms run on synthetic/simulated 90-day telemetry, not production data, so gains are comparative-in-simulation (§3, p. 8). Headline results: MTTD fell from 6-12 h (traditional) to 30-90 min (agentic) and MTTR from 12-24 h to 2-6 h, reported as 75% and 80% improvements (§4, p. 13; Table 3, p. 14), with markedly lower MTTR variance and tail latency (Fig. 4, p. 13). A second summary table reports different magnitudes/units — MTTD 18.2 min -> 10.2 min (44%) and MTTR 32.5 min -> 17.2 min (47%) (Table 9, p. 20) — an internal inconsistency with Table 3; the text also cites 34-47% improvement in time-based efficiency measures (§4, p. 19). In a simulated zero-day scenario, total response/containment time dropped from 42 min to 9 min (76% reduction; Table 10, pp. 20-21).
General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: Conceptually, the paper sharpens the distinction between rule-based/scripted automation (SOAR) and agentic autonomy — goal-directed behaviour, contextual reasoning, dynamic action selection and outcome-based strategy adaptation (§1, p. 3; §2, p. 5). It contributes a governance model of 'bounded autonomy': autonomy delivers the largest gains in high-volume, low-context routine alert handling, while high-severity, ambiguous, business-impacting incidents still require human judgment at strategic checkpoints (§4, p. 17; §5, p. 24). It evidences a structural redistribution of knowledge work — analysts move from execution to supervision, auditing and exception handling, requiring new AI-oversight skills (§4, pp. 15-16; §5, p. 24) — and frames agentic SOCs as socio-technical, knowledge-intensive systems from an IKM perspective (§1, p. 3; §6, p. 26). It is a single agentic overlay with tiered autonomous remediation actions rather than an explicit multi-agent LLM system; implementation details of the agents (models, algorithms) are not specified (§3, pp. 10-11).
Limitations / Future Work: Authors acknowledge external-validity constraints of synthetic telemetry: it cannot reproduce the ambiguity of novel attacks requiring human intuition, and the simulation omits organisational factors such as team dynamics and communication overhead (§3, p. 8). The Experience dimension relies on system-based proxies and modelled interactions — no direct analyst survey — so subjective perceptions (trust, fatigue) are not directly captured and some experience indicators are themselves simulated (§3, pp. 6, 10; §4, p. 19). Additional observed weaknesses: MTTD/MTTR baselines differ in scale between Table 3 (hours; p. 14) and Table 9 (minutes; p. 20) without reconciliation, and the agentic system's implementation (algorithms, models, LLM usage) is not described in reproducible detail (§3, pp. 10-11). Adoption barriers identified: fragmented telemetry, legacy data formats, distrust of AI decisions and organisational reluctance to delegate authority (§5, p. 25). Future work: integrating explainable AI mechanisms, longitudinal real-world deployments and refined human-control/governance mechanisms (§6, p. 26).
Relevance to My Thesis: Directly relevant: the study quantifies (in simulation) how agentic AI reduces MTTD and MTTR in SOC incident response against an analyst-centric baseline — exactly the thesis's dependent variables — and its 'bounded autonomy' human-in-the-loop model (§4, p. 17; Fig. 3, p. 11) is adjacent to the agentic-copilot paradigm in which the human retains decision authority. The 3E framework (Efficiency/Effectiveness/Experience) and its RQ-to-metric mapping (Table 1, p. 7) offer a reusable evaluation template for the dissertation's measurement design, and the triage-bottleneck evidence (FPR 0.544 in manual triage; Table 5, p. 14) supports the copilot-value argument. Evidential weight is tempered by the synthetic nature of the telemetry and by internal metric inconsistencies (Tables 3 vs. 9). The study enters the corpus with the mandatory stratum caveat (Qualis A3 — PDR-0007).
Relevance Score: High — it is one of the few studies that empirically compares traditional vs. agentic SOC workflows with MTTD/MTTR as primary endpoints (Tables 3, 9, 10) and proposes an evaluation framework directly reusable by the thesis. The score reflects thematic centrality; evidence strength is moderated by the synthetic/simulated data and the Qualis A3 stratum caveat (PDR-0007).

Title: Design of a Security Framework for Multi-Agent Systems Based on Model Context Protocol in SOC Environments (title page, p. 1).
Authors: Rodrigo Tavares de Pina Simões; Xavier Larriva-Novo; Carmen Sánchez-Zas; Victor A. Villagrá; Andrés I. Marín López — Departamento de Ingeniería de Sistemas Telemáticos, ETSI Telecomunicación, Universidad Politécnica de Madrid, Spain (p. 1). The artifact derives from the first author's Master's thesis implementation at UPM (ref. [34], p. 31).
Year & Venue: 2026 — Applied Sciences (MDPI), vol. 16, article 7915, DOI 10.3390/app16167915; received 14 July 2026, published 8 August 2026, open access CC BY (p. 1).
Core Problem Addressed: SOCs depend on Level 1 analysts for alert triage under growing alert volumes, alert fatigue, and tool fragmentation, which opens windows for lateral movement and exfiltration before response starts (§1, p. 2). LLM-based multi-agent systems using MCP are being adopted to automate these Level 1 tasks, but their autonomy and tool access expose attack classes with no direct analog in traditional software security — tool poisoning, tool shadowing, indirect prompt injection, memory poisoning, inter-agent trust exploitation, and confused deputy attacks (Abstract, p. 1; §1, p. 2). Existing taxonomies (OWASP LLM/Agentic Top 10, OWASP MCP Top 10, MITRE ATLAS, ATFAA) systematize these risks but offer no consensus mechanism to translate them into deployable middleware controls, and no prior work combines a functional multi-agent SOC architecture on a real SIEM with a systematically derived, experimentally validated security framework (§1, pp. 2-3; Table 1, pp. 4-5).
Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: A security framework for MCP-based multi-agent SOC pipelines, implemented as a middleware gateway interposed between agents and MCP servers, through which no agent can invoke any tool directly (§3.2, p. 7). It comprises a connection-phase tool registration validator (description regex scan, namespace-ownership anti-shadowing check, SHA-256 manifest pinning against rug-pull; §3.2.1, p. 8) plus five execution layers: L1 runtime RBAC, L2 rate limiting (20-30 calls/60 s per role; 10 approval requests/hour against oversight saturation and consent fatigue), L3 input validation (JSON Schema + injection scans on tool arguments, inter-agent handoffs, memory context with per-session namespacing, and external data), L4 output validation (injection/exfiltration/self-propagation patterns, 100 KB size cap), and L5 append-only audit log with SHA-256 hashing of sensitive fields (§3.2.2-3.2.6, pp. 9-12), plus transversal controls (failure opacity, version pinning, session UUIDs, supply-chain binary hashing, channel authentication; §3.2.7, p. 12). The protected agentic system is a sequential three-agent triage-enrichment-response pipeline (GPT-4o mini agents with role-specialized allowlists over 16 Wazuh tools: 3 triage, 7 enrichment, 6 response) with persistent shared memory, connected to a real Wazuh SIEM through a custom MCP server; the response agent never executes actions directly — it produces a structured plan with human approval and escalation flags (HITL), and propose_wazuh_rule only returns a proposal for analyst review (§3.1, pp. 5-6).
Methodology: Design-and-experimental-validation study: (i) threat model of 35 attack vectors selected from five taxonomies under explicit architectural-relevance, empirical-grounding, and SOC-applicability inclusion rules, of which 29 are middleware-addressable and covered (§3.2.8, pp. 12-13; Table 2, p. 13); (ii) laboratory implementation in Python 3.11/FastAPI with GPT-4o mini (temperature 0.1), a Rust Wazuh MCP server (Streamable HTTP, MCP 2025-06-18), Wazuh 4.14.0 on Vagrant, and Docker Compose with three isolated network segments (§3.3, pp. 15-17; Table 4, p. 17); (iii) controlled evaluation via a purpose-built, specification-compliant malicious MCP server (4 end-to-end attack tools) plus test-harness injections, organized into six suites T00-T05 with 25 unique attack instances repeated N=20 times, yielding 600 block decisions, each paired with legitimate cases for the false-block metric (§3.4-3.5, pp. 18-23; Table 5, p. 20); complemented by a full-pipeline demonstration under unprotected vs. secured conditions (§4.2, pp. 23-24), per-control micro-benchmarks (N=10,000; §4.3, p. 24), an obfuscation-robustness probe (§4.4, p. 25), and a false-positive probe on attack-like benign SOC traffic (§4.5, pp. 25-26). Design alignment is externally checked against the OWASP Practical Guide for Secure MCP Server Development v1.0 (Table 3, p. 14). Code is openly available (p. 29).
Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: Not specified quantitatively — the paper does not measure MTTD or MTTR and performs no empirical time-to-detect/time-to-respond comparison against a baseline; its motivation invokes triage delay and alert fatigue only qualitatively (§1, p. 2). What is actually measured is security efficacy and overhead of the middleware: 600/600 attack block decisions, 0 bypasses, and 0 false blocks on the evaluated legitimate set across six suites (Table 12, §4.1, p. 23); a full-pipeline demonstration where decision-relevant response-plan fields were identical between unprotected and secured conditions for a real Wazuh alert and a synthetic SSH brute-force alert, i.e., the security layer preserves benign operational output (§4.2, pp. 23-24); and per-call processing cost below 0.6 ms (below 30 µs with schema precompilation), three to four orders of magnitude smaller than one LLM invocation, so the protection adds negligible latency to the automated triage-enrichment-response loop (Table 13, §4.3, p. 24). Counter-evidence bounding the result: all four obfuscation techniques fully evade the lexical L3/L4 scans (Table 14, §4.4, p. 25) and 7 of 8 attack-like benign SOC inputs are falsely blocked by the isolated L3 argument scan (Table 15, §4.5, pp. 25-26).
General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: First work to jointly deliver a functional multi-agent SOC architecture, MCP integration, an implemented middleware security framework, and experimental evaluation against controlled attacks — no reviewed prior work satisfies all four dimensions (Table 1, §2, pp. 4-5). It demonstrates that systematic middleware controls can secure MCP-based agentic deployments without modifying agents, models, or MCP servers, treating the LLM as a black box (Abstract, p. 1; §3.3, p. 16; §5, p. 26), and operationalizes recurrent design principles of the agentic-SOC literature (role specialization with least privilege, persistent shared memory, trust-boundary enforcement, HITL oversight; §2, p. 3). It shows pre-admission inspection of tool metadata is implementable and effective against tool poisoning and name collision (§5, p. 26), argues deterministic (non-LLM) security decisions preserve reproducibility and avoid reintroducing the prompt-injection surface (§3.2, p. 8), and offers a portability recipe for other linear agent pipelines via four configuration points (§3.3, p. 17). Controls map onto the OWASP secure-MCP guidance (Table 3, p. 14) and the full stack is open-sourced (p. 29).
Limitations / Future Work: The blocking guarantee holds only for non-adaptive, in-clear payloads: all four obfuscation techniques (base64, Cyrillic homoglyphs, Spanish translation, paraphrase) completely evade the lexical L3 scan, and the two L4-detectable payloads are likewise evaded (§4.4, Table 14, p. 25); conversely, 7/8 benign attack-like SOC inputs (shell logs, file paths, tickets quoting attackers) are false positives of the isolated argument scan, so lexical matching is imprecise in both directions (§4.5, Table 15, pp. 25-26; §5, p. 27). Adaptive adversaries were not modeled and failure opacity is verified only structurally (§5, p. 26). Six of 35 vectors remain uncovered (RAG poisoning, adversarial embeddings, package hallucination out of middleware scope; consensus manipulation and covert coordination inapplicable to the sequential topology; replay requires server-side freshness checks) (§3.2.8, p. 13; §5, p. 27). The DNS-rebinding origin check was inactive in the evaluated deployment, compensated by loopback binding and network segmentation (§3.2.7, p. 12; §5, p. 27). Evaluation used a single LLM (GPT-4o mini) and a file-based memory store unsuitable for production scale (§5, p. 27). Future work: semantic/classifier/LLM-based detection (primary avenue), extension to non-sequential topologies via a transition-graph handoff validator, cross-model evaluation, production-grade deployment with SIEM-integrated audit log and real-time anomaly detection, tamper-evident hash-chained logging, and periodic re-application of the vector-selection methodology (§6, pp. 28-29).
Relevance to My Thesis: Directly relevant as the security-enablement layer for the thesis object (an agentic copilot reducing MTTD/MTTR in incident response): it is built on exactly the target scenario — LLM multi-agent triage-enrichment-response automation of SOC Level 1 work on a real SIEM, motivated by alert fatigue and response delay (§1, p. 2; §3.1, p. 5) — and answers the adoption-blocking question of how to deploy such a copilot safely, showing the guardrail layer preserves benign operational output and adds sub-millisecond overhead (§4.2-4.3, pp. 23-24). Its HITL design (response agent proposes, never executes; approval rate-limiting against consent fatigue) is a concrete pattern for the 'copilot' rather than 'autopilot' posture the thesis argues for (§3.1, p. 6; §3.2.3, p. 9). It does not, however, provide MTTD/MTTR evidence, so in the synthesis it supports the feasibility/trust dimension (RQ on architectures and safeguards) rather than the quantitative benefit dimension. P94 was the only unqualified 'Include' of RSL cycle 3.
Relevance Score: High — it is squarely in-domain (agentic multi-agent AI automating SOC incident triage-enrichment-response over a real SIEM) and uniquely combines architecture, MCP integration, and experimental validation (Table 1, pp. 4-5), making it a cornerstone for the thesis chapters on copilot architecture and deployment safeguards; the absence of MTTD/MTTR quantification is its only gap for the review's primary outcome.

Title: Agentic AI-Driven SOC-as-a-Service for Optimizing Incident Response in Cloud Environments: A Conceptual Framework (p. 1).
Authors: Abdulaziz Y. Alhumaidi; Faisal A. Al-Qadda; Albandari Alsumayt (corresponding); Majid Alshammari — Imam Abdulrahman Bin Faisal University (Saudi Aramco Cybersecurity Chair) and Taif University, Saudi Arabia (p. 1).
Year & Venue: 2026; Network (MDPI), vol. 6, issue 4, article 84; received 13 Jul 2026, accepted 21 Sep 2026, published 1 Oct 2026; DOI 10.3390/network6040084 (p. 1).
Core Problem Addressed: Cloud security operations must process high-volume, rapidly changing telemetry within short response windows while preserving governance and accountability, yet SOCs remain constrained by alert fatigue, high false-positive rates, analyst overload, staffing shortages, fragmented tooling, and slow incident handling (Abstract, p. 1; §4.3, p. 10). The literature on cloud defense, SOC modernization, RAG, and Agentic AI is fragmented, with few studies integrating governance, detection, incident response, and agentic orchestration into a cloud-centric synthesis (§1, p. 2; §4.1, p. 8). Agentic systems additionally introduce a new attack surface: untrusted telemetry, retrieved documents, and tool responses can carry direct/indirect prompt injection, retrieval poisoning, unauthorized tool use, and cross-tenant leakage (§1, p. 2; §4.7, p. 12).
Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: A two-part contribution: (a) a focused systematic review of 33 studies (23-study legacy corpus + 10 quality-appraised Scopus additions) answering RQ1-RQ5 (§2, p. 3; §3.1, pp. 3-4); and (b) a secure Agentic AI-driven SOCaaS conceptual framework with six core layers — multi-source telemetry ingestion, automated triage/enrichment, retrieval and context (RAG over playbooks, MITRE ATT&CK, cloud policies), agentic reasoning and orchestration, governance and human oversight, and response execution with audit — plus a cross-cutting security and trust-enforcement plane (§5.4, Fig. 4, p. 18; §5.4.1, pp. 18-19). The agentic layer performs goal-directed multistep reasoning, task decomposition, tool coordination, and response recommendation, but is explicitly bounded: model output is a recommendation, not an authorization; a deterministic policy gate outside the LLM decides deny/auto-execute/escalate, and high-impact actions require human approval (§5.1, p. 16; §5.4.5-5.4.6, pp. 19-20). Nine design principles cover cloud awareness, context-rich decision support, bounded orchestration, human oversight, auditability, modularity, adversarially robust context handling, least-privilege policy-mediated execution, and tenant isolation (§5.3, pp. 17-18); Table 4 maps six adversarial threats (prompt injection, retrieval poisoning, tool misuse, cross-tenant leakage, audit manipulation) to architectural controls (p. 19).
Methodology: Two-phase focused SLR with qualitative thematic synthesis (no meta-analysis due to heterogeneity): Phase 1 legacy corpus of 23 studies (IEEE Xplore, Google Scholar); Phase 2 reproducible Scopus update reported per PRISMA 2020 — 2181 records, 70 duplicates removed, 2111 screened, 65 sought, 55 not retrieved, 10 full texts assessed and all 10 included (§3.1-3.4, pp. 3-5; Fig. 1, p. 5); protocol not prospectively registered (§3.1, p. 4); full-text quality appraisal on five 0-2 criteria with a 7/10 inclusion threshold (§3.5, p. 6). The framework is then evaluated by four seeded (seed 42), openly released component-level simulations on deliberately imperfect synthetic data (3% label noise, distractor terms, logging failures): (1) Random Forest triage on 20,000 synthetic events; (2) TF-IDF lexical retrieval over 12 playbooks and 60 paraphrased incident queries; (3) discrete-event simulation of 2000 incidents, 6 analysts, comparing manual vs. narrow-AI vs. agentic+governance operating models; (4) 1000 Monte Carlo runs of the six-step privilege-escalation workflow for audit completeness (§6.1-6.5, pp. 22-28; code on GitHub/Zenodo, Data Availability, p. 32).
Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: Not demonstrated empirically — no real-world comparison against a concrete deployed baseline is executed; all response-time figures are outputs of a seeded discrete-event simulation under declared synthetic assumptions, which the authors frame as "internal feasibility rather than production efficacy" (Abstract, p. 1; §6, p. 22; §6.7, p. 29). Within the simulation (2000 incidents, 6 analysts, 12 incidents/hour): mean time to triage drops from 20.1 min (modeled manual SOC) and 7.1 min (narrow-AI) to 2.1 min in the governed agentic model, and mean time to respond from 59.5 and 23.4 min to 8.8 min — a 6.8-fold reduction vs. the modeled manual baseline — with 90th-percentile response at 16.5 vs. 101.8 min, analyst touches per incident 0.32 vs. 3.50, and 67.9% of actions auto-executed (§6.4, Table 8, pp. 25-26). Under rising load (6→26 incidents/hour) the agentic model stays flat at ~8.5-8.6 min while the manual model saturates beyond ~14/hour (up to >1655 min) and narrow-AI beyond ~22/hour (256.0 min) (Fig. 8b, p. 26). Threshold sensitivity shows near-total automation gains only ~3.3 min (9.9→6.6 min) while high-impact auto-execution rises from 0% to 74.15% (Table 9, Fig. 9, pp. 26-27). The paper uses "mean time to triage/respond", not MTTD/MTTR nomenclature, and threats-to-validity explicitly note that service times and risk-score quality are modeling assumptions, not measurements from a deployed SOC (§6.6, p. 28).
General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: The review organizes the field into three maturity levels — narrow AI detection/triage, LLM/RAG contextual support, and semi-autonomous agentic orchestration — finding the agentic level most ambitious but least validated (§4.9, Fig. 3, pp. 12-13; Table 3, p. 14). It concludes the literature favors bounded, semi-autonomous operation with human authority over full autonomy (§4.5, p. 11; §4.11, p. 16). For agent security it synthesizes benchmark/attack/defense work (AgentDojo, Agent Security Bench, MELON, AgentVigil, Prompt Infection, adaptive attacks) showing instructions propagate between agents and static defenses remain vulnerable, deriving four architectural requirements: separate instructions from data, provenance-aware retrieval from controlled sources, restricted tool access, and authorization outside the language model (§4.7, p. 12). Simulation evidence quantifies agentic design trade-offs: conservative triage gating cuts alert volume 59.5% with 4.81% threat leakage (Table 6, p. 24); retrieval grounding raises top-1 playbook mapping from 0.317 to 0.850 (Table 7, pp. 24-25); the governance threshold behaves as an organizational risk-appetite parameter with a sharply asymmetric speed-control curve (Table 9, p. 27); and audit logging costs only 1.79% mean overhead with 95.5% complete six-step evidence chains (Table 10, p. 28).
Limitations / Future Work: Review limitations: intermediate counts of the 23-study legacy phase were not preserved; 55 of 65 Scopus reports could not be retrieved (possible underrepresentation of subscription-only research); Web of Science was not searched; six legacy sources (18.2% of corpus) remain preprints; no quantitative meta-analysis was possible (§7, pp. 29-30; §3.2, p. 4). Validation limitations: the simulations establish internal feasibility only — Experiment 1 evaluates conventional ML (Random Forest), not generative agentic reasoning; Experiment 2 uses a TF-IDF lexical baseline, not dense RAG; Experiments 3-4 rest on assumed distributions; the queueing model omits LLM inference variation, hallucination loops, tool failures, and human factors; and no experiment tests prompt injection, retrieval poisoning, cross-tenant leakage, or audit tampering — the security plane "remains an architectural requirement until it is implemented and adversarially tested" (§6.6, p. 28; §7, pp. 29-30). Future work: broader database coverage, working prototypes tested in real cloud incident-response settings, comparative evaluation of narrow AI vs. LLM vs. RAG vs. agentic orchestration, policy engineering for approval thresholds and compliance-aware orchestration, and human-factors studies on trust calibration and workload (§7, p. 30).
Relevance to My Thesis: Direct topical match: the paper designs an Agentic AI orchestration layer for cloud SOC incident response whose declared purpose is faster triage and response under governance — precisely the copilot-reduces-MTTD/MTTR territory of the thesis — and it is one of the few studies that explicitly quantifies (albeit in simulation) the triage-time and response-time deltas between manual, narrow-AI, and governed agentic operating models, including a load-scaling analysis explaining *why* agentic orchestration prevents MTTR saturation (analyst-queue arrival-rate reduction) (§6.4, pp. 25-26). Its six-layer architecture, nine design principles, bounded-autonomy governance gate, and threat-to-control mapping provide a reusable architectural vocabulary for the thesis framework chapter, and its three-level maturity model situates copilot approaches within the literature (§4.9, pp. 12-13; §5.3-5.4, pp. 17-20). Inclusion with caveat: the evidence is synthetic component-level simulation of a conceptual framework — no deployed agent, no real incident data, no empirical MTTD/MTTR measurement — so its numbers inform hypothesis formation and experiment design, not effect-size claims (§6.6-6.7, pp. 28-29).
Relevance Score: High - the study sits squarely on the thesis intersection (Agentic AI copilot/orchestrator optimizing incident response time in cloud SOCs) and contributes both an SLR-grounded architecture and simulated triage/response-time comparisons across operating models. The caveat is evidentiary, not topical: all MTTD/MTTR-like gains are synthetic simulation results of a conceptual framework, to be cited as feasibility evidence only.

Title: AIDR-Cloud: An Agentic AI-Driven Incident Response Framework for Cloud Failures (title page, p. 1).
Authors: Akshay Pratinav and Archana Kataria, both affiliated with Intuit Inc, Mountain View, USA (p. 1) — an industry-authored paper, with the reference implementation deployed on the authors' own multi-region serverless environment (§IV, p. 3).
Year & Venue: 2026, SoutheastCon 2026 (IEEE SOUTHEASTCON conference series), proceedings pp. 163-168, DOI 10.1109/SOUTHEASTCON63549.2026.11476571 (p. 1, footer).
Core Problem Addressed: Modern cloud-native systems (hundreds of microservices, multi-region Kubernetes, Kafka streaming pipelines) have made operational failures more frequent, higher-impact and more opaque, while traditional incident response remains human-centric and fragile: manual correlation of siloed metrics/logs/traces across disparate dashboards, static and quickly outdated runbooks, escalation dependent on tribal knowledge, signal overload during major incidents, and a resulting human bottleneck with hero culture and on-call fatigue (Abstract, p. 1; §I, p. 1; §II, p. 2). These detection and diagnosis delays prolong outages and make remediation quality inconsistent (§I, p. 1), and existing AIOps tools remain largely advisory — symptom detection and alert correlation without end-to-end causal reasoning, policy-aware planning or guarded execution (§II and Table I, p. 2).
Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: AIDR-Cloud, an agentic incident detection-and-response framework explicitly positioned as an 'agentic SRE co-pilot' rather than a purely advisory AIOps tool (§I, p. 2; Abstract, p. 1). It has a three-layer architecture (§III, Fig. 1, pp. 2-3): a Perception Layer ingesting metrics, logs and traces with threshold/statistical anomaly detection; a Cognition Layer of five role-specialized collaborating LLM agents — Detector (groups anomalies into candidate incidents), Hypothesis (proposes candidate root causes), Validator (tests hypotheses against observability/cloud-API evidence with confidence scores), Planner (synthesizes ordered remediation plans with pre/postconditions, risk levels and rollback conditions) and Critic/Governance (reviews plans against policy, deciding autonomous vs. human-approval vs. advisory execution) — reasoning over a Neo4j cloud knowledge graph of services, regions, gateways, topics, databases and their dependency/failover edges (§III, p. 3; §IV, p. 3); and an Action Layer executing guarded, idempotent remediation via Kubernetes, cloud-provider, mesh/gateway and Kafka APIs with closed-loop telemetry feedback (§III, p. 3). A cross-cutting safety and governance framework enforces hard limits, canary rollouts, auto-rollback and explicit operator approval for high-risk operations such as region-wide failover (§III, p. 3). Agents use GPT-5 or Claude-Opus class models via tool-augmented prompts, orchestrated by a Go serverless layer, integrated with Prometheus, cloud logs and tracing; deployment starts in shadow/assist mode and graduates to autonomous execution of low-risk actions (§IV, p. 3).
Methodology: Three complementary evaluation axes (Abstract, p. 1; §V, p. 4). (1) Controlled fault-injection experiments on a multi-region Kubernetes + Kafka environment using Chaos Mesh and custom scripts (node outages, control-plane degradation, Kafka lag spikes, data-store throttling, gateway under-scaling, cross-region latency spikes), with multiple independent runs per fault type in a baseline configuration — experienced SREs using standard observability dashboards and runbooks — versus a treatment configuration with AIDR-Cloud as primary responder and humans in oversight; measured outcomes: MTTD, MTTR, RCA latency, RCA correctness vs. ground truth, remediation success, escalation beyond approval gates, and manual operator actions, under comparable traffic conditions (§V.A, p. 4). (2) A declared statistical methodology: bootstrap two-sided 95% confidence intervals, paired t-tests or Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, effect sizes, and an a priori power analysis (§V.B, p. 4) — though the paper states precise run counts and CIs 'can be reported in tabular form' without actually tabulating them. (3) Cost/latency decomposition into perception, cognition and action components with an LLM token-based cost model (§V.D, Table II, pp. 4-5), plus a multi-week hybrid-mode production deployment comparing AIDR-Cloud-assisted vs. human-only real incidents and postmortem quality (§V.E, p. 5).
Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: Executed empirical comparison against a concrete human-SRE baseline (Art. I satisfied). Synthetic fault-injection: MTTR falls 'from a baseline on the order of tens of minutes to single-digit minutes in many cases', with bootstrap CIs for the difference in means excluding zero, RCA explanations reached 'several times faster' than humans, tighter MTTR distributions (less variance), and statistically and practically significant reductions in MTTR and RCA latency (§V.C, p. 4). Production deployment (Table III, §V.E, p. 5): MTTD p90 reduced from 30 min pre-deployment to 5 min with AIDR-Cloud (-83%); MTTR p90 reduced from 240 min to 20 min (-91%). Aggregate conclusion figures (§VIII, p. 6): MTTR reduced by approximately 63%, root-cause analysis accelerated ~3x, human escalations decreased 65%, correct remediations selected in roughly 70% of scenarios, with no unsafe actions executed. Overhead: cognition adds reasoning latency on the order of seconds versus minutes of recovery time saved (§V.D, p. 4; §VI, p. 5), at an LLM cost of $0.079 +/- $0.024 per incident (12,400 +/- 3,200 input tokens, 2,800 +/- 890 output tokens; Table II, p. 5). Note the paper reports -63% as the overall MTTR reduction (§VIII) alongside the -91% p90 figure for real incidents (Table III); exact per-scenario synthetic values are described qualitatively, not tabulated.
General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: Demonstrates a complete perception-cognition-action agentic loop in production-grade cloud operations: role-specialized LLM agents (Detector/Hypothesis/Validator/Planner/Critic) grounded in a domain knowledge graph for explicit causal reasoning, with guarded closed-loop actuation — advancing beyond advisory AIOps recommendation engines (Table I and §II, p. 2). Shows that a layered safety and governance framework (policy engine, canary, auto-rollback, tiered human approval, full audit logging) can make partial autonomy safe, with zero unsafe actions reported (Abstract, p. 1; §III, p. 3; §VIII, p. 6). Contributes a reusable cost/latency accounting template for agentic systems (token-level cost model, seconds of reasoning overhead traded for minutes of MTTR; §V.D, pp. 4-5) and evidence of a virtuous feedback loop in which agent participation enriches the knowledge graph, runbooks and postmortems over time (§V.E, p. 5; §VI, pp. 5-6). Frames agentic AI as 'a statistically well-characterized and cost-conscious SRE co-pilot' (Abstract, p. 1).
Limitations / Future Work: Acknowledged limitations (§VI, pp. 5-6): hypotheses are incomplete or overly narrow for novel failure modes or external dependencies not represented in the knowledge graph, so human expertise remains essential; reliance on observability means missing or misleading telemetry creates blind spots; organizations with very high incident volumes or strict cost constraints must calibrate LLM usage (mixing high-capability and lighter models or rules). Reviewer-noted reporting gaps: despite the declared statistical rigor, precise run counts, confidence intervals and per-scenario synthetic numbers are never tabulated (§V.B-V.C, p. 4), the real-incident comparison is pre/post rather than randomized (Table III, p. 5), and the single-organization, vendor-authored deployment (Intuit; §IV, p. 3) limits external validity. Future work (§VII, p. 6): reinforcement learning or retrieval-augmented prompting to learn from historical incidents; broader incident taxonomy and graph coverage (serverless functions, batch pipelines, third-party and cross-organizational dependencies); evolution from reactive responder to proactive risk forecasting and preemptive mitigation; standardized schemas for inter-organizational sharing of anonymized incident learnings.
Relevance to My Thesis: Directly on-construct: the paper's own framing is an agentic 'SRE co-pilot' that reduces detection and recovery times in cloud incident response (Abstract, p. 1; §VIII, p. 6), matching the thesis object (agentic copilot reducing MTTD/MTTR in incident response). It is one of the four primary studies in the first cluster that report nominal MTTD/MTTR values against an executed concrete baseline (experienced human SREs with dashboards and runbooks, §V.A, p. 4; Table III, p. 5), satisfying RSL Art. I for comparative-benefit claims, and it adds rare production-deployment evidence plus per-incident cost accounting useful to the thesis's feasibility argument. It enters the corpus with the mandatory stratum caveat: the IEEE SOUTHEASTCON series is a B2-stratum venue, so inclusion carries the qualification formalized in PDR-0006/0007.
Relevance Score: High — it provides exactly the evidence class the thesis needs: nominal MTTD/MTTR deltas (MTTD p90 -83%, MTTR p90 -91% in production, Table III, p. 5; ~-63% MTTR overall, §VIII, p. 6) from an executed comparison against a human-SRE baseline, for an explicitly co-pilot-framed agentic system. The score is tempered only by the B2 venue stratum (mandatory caveat per PDR-0006/0007) and by incomplete tabulation of the declared statistics, not by relevance.

Title: Event-Driven Agentic SOC (ED-ASOC): Supervisor-Based LLM Framework for Dynamic Incident Response and SOAR Orchestration (title page, p. 1).
Authors: Enes Özgözler (Department of Computer Engineering, Bahçeşehir University, İstanbul, Türkiye); Asaf Varol (Engineering Management & Technology, University of Tennessee at Chattanooga, US, and Department of Computer Engineering, Maltepe University, İstanbul, TR); İhsan Tanrıverdi (Department of Computer Engineering, Bahçeşehir University, İstanbul, Türkiye) (p. 1).
Year & Venue: 2026; 2026 14th International Symposium on Digital Forensics and Security (ISDFS), IEEE; DOI 10.1109/ISDFS69419.2026.11458922 (p. 1, header/footer).
Core Problem Addressed: SOCs face a widening gap between alert volume and the speed of traditional incident response: high false-positive rates cause analyst cognitive overload, alert fatigue, and missed critical threats (Abstract, p. 1; §I, p. 1). Current SOAR platforms automate routine tasks but depend on polling-based data retrieval (e.g., every 30-60 s) and static, rule-based playbooks that cannot adapt to polymorphic malware, zero-day exploits, or living-off-the-land techniques (§I, p. 1; §III.A, p. 2). The polling delay opens a critical vulnerability window for ransomware and APT lateral movement that can occur within minutes of compromise, and existing AI deployments in security remain passive (query generation, log summarization) — unable to interact with the environment, so every action bottlenecks on human intervention (§I, p. 1).
Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: ED-ASOC, a five-layer event-driven framework (ingestion, reasoning, knowledge management, execution, governance) centered on a Supervisor Agent — an autonomous LLM-powered decision engine with actionable intelligence that interacts directly with firewalls, EDR agents, and identity providers (§I, p. 1; §III, Fig. 1, p. 2). Components: (1) a Webhook push-based ingestion layer replacing periodic polling, SIEM-agnostic (Splunk, ELK, FortiSIEM, Azure Sentinel) via JSON payloads (§III.A, p. 2); (2) the Supervisor Agent's three-stage pipeline — contextual classification by semantic similarity against the RAG knowledge base, severity assessment from asset criticality and organizational risk profiles, and remediation synthesis via structured chain-of-thought — with historical correlation against 2,847 indexed incident patterns (§III.B, pp. 2-3); (3) RAG-enhanced dynamic playbook generation from a vector database of historical incidents, security policies, and SOPs, replacing static if-then logic (§III.C, Table I, p. 3); (4) a SOAR Tool Calling interface with a registry of 47 functions in five categories (network controls, endpoint actions, identity management, ticket operations, forensic collection), each bound to strict JSON schemas with validation, rollback procedures, and atomic execution guarantees (§III.D, Table II, p. 3; §III.E, p. 3); (5) a tiered Human-in-the-Loop mechanism — low-risk actions fully automatic, medium-risk auto with notification, high-risk blocked pending analyst approval with natural-language justification (§III.E, Table III, p. 3). The agentic role is explicitly executive: the agent autonomously performs remediation (IP blocking, endpoint isolation, user suspension, file quarantine) through defined API schemas, closing the detection-to-containment gap (Abstract, p. 1; Table II, p. 3).
Methodology: Design-and-evaluate study with empirical comparison in a controlled simulated testbed emulating an enterprise SOC: FortiSIEM 7.1.1 on VMware ESXi receiving logs from 12 simulated network segments; FortiSOAR 7.4.1 with custom connectors for firewall, EDR, and Active Directory; Claude 3.5 Sonnet as LLM backend (average response latency 1.2 s); Chroma DB holding 2,847 historical incident records and 156 organizational policy documents (§IV.A, p. 3). Synthetic dataset of 1,247 security events across five MITRE ATT&CK categories — Brute Force T1110 (312; 25.0%), Phishing T1566 (287; 23.0%), Lateral Movement T1021 (198; 15.9%), Data Exfiltration T1041 (243; 19.5%), Privilege Escalation T1068 (207; 16.6%) — injected with randomized Poisson timing (λ = 4.2 events/minute) (§IV.B, p. 3). Two executed baselines: a polling-based configuration and a non-agentic LLM-Assist baseline using the same underlying LLM for advisory analysis only, with analysts manually implementing recommended actions (§IV.C, pp. 3-4; Table IV, p. 4). Metrics: detection latency, average MTTR, classification accuracy, auto-resolution rate; no statistical significance testing is reported.
Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: Executed empirical comparison against two concrete baselines (satisfies RSL Art. I). MTTD proxy (mean detection latency): 0.85 s for ED-ASOC vs 34.2 s for the polling baseline — a 97.5% reduction — and 33.8 s for LLM-Assist (§IV.C, pp. 3-4; Table IV, p. 4). MTTR: average 71.7 s vs 258.4 s for polling, a 72.3% reduction (§IV.C, p. 3; Table IV, p. 4; §VI, p. 5), and 62.3% reduction relative to LLM-Assist (190.4 s), isolating the agentic action layer's contribution (§IV.C, p. 4; §V.D, p. 5). The Abstract rounds these as '73% reduction in MTTR' and '89% decrease in detection latency' (Abstract, p. 1); the 89% figure matches the Discussion's analytical model (T_proc = 847 ms vs a 60-s polling interval, '89% latency reduction', §V.A, p. 4), while the Results section reports 97.5%. Secondary operational metrics: auto-resolution 45.5% (ED-ASOC) vs 12.3% (LLM-Assist) vs 0% (polling) — a 33.2-percentage-point agentic gain (Table IV, p. 4; §VI, p. 5); classification accuracy 91.3% vs 84.2% vs 78.4% (Table IV, p. 4); Tier-1 analyst intervention reduced by approximately 45% (567/45.5% fully automated, 412/33.0% notification-only, 268/21.5% approval-required events) (§IV.C, p. 4). Caveats: all figures come from 1,247 synthetic events in a simulated single-vendor testbed, and the second-scale MTTR measures machine-speed containment rather than a full organizational incident lifecycle (§IV.A-B, p. 3; §V.D, pp. 4-5).
General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: The LLM-Assist baseline functions as an ablation separating 'LLM-as-advisor' from 'LLM-as-actor': the LLM backbone alone improves classification (84.2% vs 78.4%) but leaves MTTD/MTTR nearly unchanged (33.8 s latency, 190.4 s MTTR), so the agentic action layer — event-driven ingestion, autonomous tool calling, structured SOAR integration — contributes the majority of operational gains (§IV.C, pp. 3-4; Table IV, p. 4). For safe autonomy, a three-tier validation pipeline (RAG grounding on Chroma DB, JSON schema constraining of every SOAR invocation, semantic consistency check against the alert context) is claimed to achieve 94% hallucination reduction, combining probabilistic reasoning with deterministic safety guarantees (§V.B, p. 4). Latency is formalized as L_total = I_p/2 + T_proc, with event-driven operation collapsing it to T_proc ≈ 847 ms and cutting idle resource consumption by 78% (§V.A, p. 4). Governance data shows calibrated oversight: of 268 high-risk decisions presented, analysts modified 23 (8.6%) and rejected 7 (2.6%) (§IV.C, p. 4). Architecturally the system is single-agent with claimed horizontal scaling beyond 10,000 events/minute behind a load balancer; the authors position a future hierarchical multi-agent design (Orchestrator delegating to Network Forensics, Malware Analysis, and Cloud Security sub-agents with domain-specific RAG bases) to reduce per-agent context-window pressure, extending DeepAgent-style agentic workflow patterns to the security domain (§V.C, p. 4).
Limitations / Future Work: Authors acknowledge five limitations (§V.D, pp. 4-5): (1) the single-agent architecture may hit throughput constraints above 10,000 events/minute — to be addressed by hierarchical multi-agent coordination; (2) the RAG knowledge base requires periodic updates — future automated threat-intelligence ingestion pipelines; (3) adversarial robustness against prompt injection targeting the LLM controller remains open, requiring input sanitization and adversarial training; (4) evaluation relies on a synthetic 1,247-event dataset rather than production SOC traffic, so real-world validation is needed to strengthen generalizability; (5) only two baselines were run — intermediate semi-autonomous configurations with selective tool execution would clarify the autonomy-performance tradeoff. Future work also includes privacy-preserving threat-intelligence sharing protocols (§VI, p. 5). Not acknowledged: absence of statistical significance testing, dependence on a single LLM backend (Claude 3.5 Sonnet) and a single-vendor Fortinet stack, and MTTR defined at machine timescale (seconds) in a controlled environment.
Relevance to My Thesis: Direct and central: ED-ASOC instantiates exactly the thesis object — an agentic LLM copilot/supervisor reducing MTTD and MTTR in incident response — and is one of the four primary studies in the cluster reporting nominal MTTD/MTTR gains against an executed baseline (72.3% MTTR reduction and 97.5% detection-latency reduction vs polling; 62.3% MTTR reduction vs a non-agentic LLM-Assist; §IV.C, Table IV, pp. 3-4). The LLM-Assist ablation is especially valuable for the dissertation's argument, since it quantifies the marginal contribution of agentic autonomy (copilot-as-actor) over advisory LLM use (copilot-as-advisor), and the tiered HITL matrix (Table III, p. 3) plus analyst modification/rejection rates (§IV.C, p. 4) inform the copilot governance discussion. Mandatory stratum caveat: the venue is in the B4 series (PDR-0006/0007), so the evidential weight is discounted accordingly; moreover, all evidence comes from a simulated testbed with synthetic MITRE ATT&CK events, not production SOC traffic (§IV.A-B, p. 3; §V.D, p. 5), so the numbers should be cited as controlled-environment results.
Relevance Score: High - the study answers the thesis question head-on with executed baseline comparisons quantifying agentic-copilot reductions in detection latency and MTTR, including an ablation isolating the autonomy layer; weight is tempered by the B4-series venue stratum (PDR-0006/0007) and simulated-testbed-only evidence.

Title: Intelligent Site Reliability Engineering: A Multi-agent LLM Framework for Automated Incident Analysis and Root Cause Determination (title page, p. 1).
Authors: Vipin Kataria (Picarro Inc, USA; corresponding e-mail vipink2@illinois.edu) — single-author industry paper (p. 1).
Year & Venue: 2025 — International Journal of Intelligent Engineering and Systems (IJIES), Vol. 18, No. 11, pp. 450-466, DOI 10.22266/ijies2025.1231.28; received 2025-09-04, revised 2025-10-14; CC BY-SA 4.0 license (header, p. 1). Venue is NOT INDEXED in the review's quality strata (Qualis/SJR) — mandatory stratum caveat per PDR-0007.
Core Problem Addressed: Modern distributed systems generate 10,000-50,000 daily alerts, causing alert fatigue and delayed incident response; SRE teams spend 60-80% of their time on manual investigation, and MTTR inflates from a typical 30-45 minutes to over 2-3 hours for complex distributed failures (§1, p. 1). Threshold-based alerting yields 60-85% false positives in dynamic cloud environments, manual correlation does not scale beyond 100-200 microservices, and traditional ML-based AIOps reaches only 45-65% root-cause accuracy because it pattern-matches without semantic understanding (§1, p. 2; §2.2, p. 3). Existing single-LLM operational tools lack the specialized domain expertise needed across logs, metrics, traces and infrastructure (§2.5, p. 4).
Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: The Intelligent SRE Agent: a hierarchical four-layer multi-agent LLM framework in which an LLM-powered Master Agent (Claude-4 Sonnet) performs natural-language reasoning and investigation planning and orchestrates five domain-specialized agents — Logs, Metrics, Traces, Infrastructure and ML Services — via the Model Context Protocol (MCP) (§3.1, p. 4). Orchestration is prompt-driven and adaptive (planning, agent selection, introspection), with empirically observed confidence thresholds above 0.85 and 3-7 investigation rounds (§3.3, pp. 5-6); a four-phase workflow goes from alert interpretation to a diagnostic report with root cause, confidence scores and remediation recommendations (§3.7, p. 7). The agentic role is explicitly a copilot: default deployment is read-only advisory mode, with human-in-the-loop approval for P0/P1 incidents, hallucination mitigation via confidence scoring (<0.7 flagged), minimum 3-agent cross-validation, evidence grounding, circuit breakers and audit logging (§3.8, pp. 7-8).
Methodology: Empirical dual-testbed evaluation with systematic chaos engineering: a primary controlled testbed (7-microservice IoT sensor pipeline, 150 injected failure scenarios over 8 weeks, 1,000 concurrent connections, single AWS region) and an extended production-replica staging environment (50+ microservices, 200 scenarios over 10 weeks, 5,000 connections, multi-AZ, heterogeneous stack) (§4.1, Table 1, p. 8). Failures were injected with Toxiproxy, Chaos Monkey, Litmus Chaos and custom injection (Table 2, p. 9) across five categories: infrastructure, application services, data pipeline, external dependencies and configuration (Table 3, p. 9). Executed baseline: parallel manual incident analysis by three senior SRE engineers (5+ years of distributed-systems experience), each incident analyzed independently by all three with consensus-based ground truth (§4.1.3 'Baseline Comparison', p. 10). Cross-LLM validation replicated the framework over Claude-4 Sonnet, GPT-4 Turbo, Gemini Pro and Llama-3-70B (Table 9, p. 13).
Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: MTTD is measured directly as Mean Time to Diagnosis against an executed manual baseline (Art. I satisfied): 47.2 min (manual, 3 senior SREs) reduced to 8.5 min in the primary testbed — the 82% reduction claimed in the abstract and conclusion (Abstract, p. 1; §5.1, p. 14) — and to 11.2 min in the extended 50+ microservice validation, reported as a 79.1% overall reduction across both testbeds (Table 4, p. 10). Root-cause accuracy rose from 67.3% (manual) to 92.1% (primary) and 89.4% (extended); historical incident-matching precision from 43.1% to 96.3%/93.7%; false-positive rate fell from 28.7% to 4.2%/6.8% (Table 4, p. 10). Case studies show 8.3-16.4 min automated diagnosis vs 45-142 min manual (79.1-88.5% improvement; Table 7, p. 12), and per-category MTTD of 6.2-15.9 min (Table 5, p. 10). MTTR proper (time to resolution) is NOT measured — it appears only as motivating context (30-45 min to 2-3 h, §1, p. 1); the benefit evidenced is on the diagnosis stage of the incident-response pipeline.
General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: Claims the first multi-agent LLM framework designed specifically for comprehensive incident analysis in distributed systems, with MCP-based dynamic orchestration as a reusable architectural pattern (§1 contributions, p. 2). Provides comparative evidence that domain specialization outperforms single-LLM AIOps (92.1% vs ~60-80% for single-model frameworks; Table 8, pp. 12-13) and that the architecture abstracts the underlying model: accuracy 84.2-92.1% and agent-coordination success 92.3-98.7% across four LLM providers (Table 9, p. 13), supporting vendor-independent deployment. Its production-safety stack (confidence scoring, multi-agent validation, evidence grounding, human-in-the-loop, advisory-first staged rollout; §3.8, pp. 7-8) is a concrete blueprint for operating agentic AI in critical infrastructure.
Limitations / Future Work: Scaling from 7 to 50+ microservices degrades performance (-2.7 pp accuracy, +2.7 min diagnosis time; §5.2, p. 14); external-dependency failures have the lowest accuracy (85.3-88.0%; Table 5, p. 10); the Traces Agent suffers the largest scalability impact (+74% response time; Table 6, p. 11; §5.2, p. 14); and the LLM-driven orchestration lacks a formal theoretical model, with non-deterministic behavior validated only empirically (§3.3, pp. 5-6; §5.2, p. 14). Additional caveats: evaluation uses injected failures on controlled/staging testbeds, not live production incidents (Table 1, p. 8); single-author industry paper; MTTR end-to-end is not measured. Future work: formal mathematical models of coordination, validation at 100+ microservices, advanced adversarial/hallucination safeguards, predictive incident prevention, and federated learning across organizations (§5.4, p. 14).
Relevance to My Thesis: Direct and central: it is one of the four primary studies in the review's nominal MTTD/MTTR cluster backed by an executed baseline comparison, quantifying an agentic multi-agent LLM copilot that cuts MTTD by 82% (47.2 -> 8.5 min) against a concrete manual baseline of three senior SREs (Table 4, p. 10; Abstract, p. 1). Its human-in-the-loop, advisory-first deployment model (§3.8.3-3.8.4, p. 8) matches the thesis framing of a copilot (not autopilot) for incident response, and its MCP orchestration and safety mechanisms inform the thesis architecture discussion. Mandatory stratum caveat (PDR-0007): IJIES is NOT INDEXED in the review's quality strata, so its evidence is weighted accordingly; note also that the gain is on MTTD (diagnosis), with MTTR not directly measured.
Relevance Score: High — it is one of the few included primaries with an executed empirical baseline (3 senior SREs, consensus ground truth) and explicit MTTD quantification (-82%, Table 4, p. 10) for an agentic LLM copilot in incident response, the exact phenomenon of the thesis. Weight is tempered by the non-indexed venue (PDR-0007) and testbed-only (non-production) validation.

Title: DevAIOps: A Systematic Literature Review on Integrating Explainable AI Agents into CI/CD Pipelines for Optimization, Security, and Auto-Remediation (title page, p. 344).
Authors: Othmane Ait Ami (corresponding author, othmane.aitami-etu@etu.univh2c.ma), Abderrazak Boumahdi, Mohamed Azmi — Digital Engineering for Leading Technologies and Automation (DELTA), ENSAM, Hassan II University, Casablanca, Morocco (p. 344).
Year & Venue: 2026 — Procedia Computer Science, Vol. 290, pp. 344-351 (Elsevier, open access CC BY-NC-ND), proceedings of the 23rd International Conference on Mobile Systems and Pervasive Computing (MobiSPC), August 18-20, 2026, Athens, Greece (p. 344). Mandatory stratum caveat per PDR-0006/0007: Procedia Computer Science is an A4-stratum conference-proceedings series, below the review's A1-A2/Q1-Q2 quality bar — admissible only under the R1 foundational-conditional rule for secondary studies.
Core Problem Addressed: CI/CD pipelines have grown beyond manual human management: failure causes are buried in massive logs, monitoring data overwhelms operators, and AI-generated remediation advice must be validated before deployment (§1, p. 345). Embedding autonomous AI agents in vital pipelines introduces new challenges — hallucination in LLM-based remediation recommendations, non-transparency of automated decisions, and lack of frameworks for securing agent behavior (§1, p. 345). The paper coins 'DevAIOps' for explainable, controllable AI agents in DevOps/DevSecOps workflows affecting KPIs such as MTTR, deployment success rate and security compliance (§1, p. 345), and cites a generative-AI-in-DevOps market of USD 942.5M (2022) projected to USD 22.1B by 2032 at 38.2% CAGR [11] (§1, p. 345). Three RQs cover AI/ML/LLM techniques in CI/CD and AIOps (RQ1), explainability in AI-driven DevOps automation (RQ2), and security risks of LLM-based autonomous remediation, including hallucinations (RQ3) (§1, p. 345).
Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: As an SLR, the paper's contribution is conceptual, not a system: a reproducible review over 217 unique records, a thematic taxonomy over five dimensions (T1 AIOps, T2 AI-driven CI/CD optimization, T3 DevSecOps, T4 XAI in software operations, T5 LLM agents for autonomous software operations), a four-gap analysis, and a research agenda (§1, p. 345; §2.1, p. 346). It motivates a reference DevAIOps architecture (Fig. 1, p. 345) and, for the two trust gaps, proposes a 'trust loop' in which artifact-linked explanations feed OWASP-aligned multi-layer validation and risk-tiered human-in-the-loop gating before any remediation is applied (Abstract, p. 344; Fig. 4, p. 350). The Agentic AI role is synthesized from reviewed primaries: LLM agents (theme T5) for incident RCA, outage summarization and auto-remediation — e.g., ReAct-style tool-using agents [9] — with the proposed research direction of specialized agents for build, security and remediation governed under one explainability layer (Gap 1, §4.1, p. 349).
Methodology: SECONDARY STUDY — PRISMA-guided SLR (§2, p. 346). Sources: Scopus, Web of Science, plus manually sourced seminal papers; date range January 2019-April 2026, query run 19 April 2026, English only, searched in title/abstract/keywords; example query ('AIOps' OR 'AI-driven DevOps' OR 'CI/CD') AND ('large language model' OR 'LLM agent' OR 'explainable AI' OR 'auto-remediation') (Table 1, §2.1, p. 346). Funnel: 222 candidate publications → 217 unique records → 47 eligible studies → 10 high-impact studies (2019-2025) synthesized in depth (Abstract, p. 344; Fig. 2, p. 347). Ranking used a scripted composite relevance score (0-100) with seven weighted components: citation impact, influential citations, venue quality, recency, open access, tier-1 and tier-2 keywords (Table 2, §2.2, pp. 346-347). Quality assessment used five QA criteria (0/0.5/1.0 each); all ten in-depth studies scored >= 4.0/5.0, seven at the maximum (§2.3, p. 347). Corpus composition: 61% empirical, 26% secondary, 13% conceptual (§3, p. 348). Screening was single-reviewer, partially mitigated by the deterministic scoring algorithm (§5, p. 350).
Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: Secondary evidence only — the review runs no experiment of its own and states that all quantitative figures (such as MTTR decreases) are reported as stated by the original researchers (§5 Conclusion validity, p. 351). MTTR numbers aggregated from reviewed primaries: Zhang et al. [3] (GPT-4 in-context learning for cloud-incident RCA) report 35% higher accuracy than rule-based approaches and a 42% MTTR reduction for RCA in production; Goel et al. [6] (X-Lifecycle, cross-phase attention over SDLC data) report 28% fewer false positives and 31% end-to-end MTTR reduction; Jin et al. [8] report 78% of LLM outage summaries rated helpful by on-call engineers; Roy et al. [9] report 68% top-1 RCA accuracy for a five-tool ReAct agent vs 45% for non-agent methods (§3.5, p. 349). Fu et al. [10] report ML-based runtime anomaly detection reducing incident response time by 65% (§3.3, p. 349). Crucially, the review itself flags (Gap 2) that the 31-55% MTTR improvements in Microsoft studies [3][6][8] rest on proprietary infrastructure, are not externally verifiable, and that no standard MTTR/KPI benchmarks exist (§4.1, pp. 349-350). No MTTD figures are reported anywhere in the paper, and no comparative benefit can be attributed to this paper's own work.
General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: The paper names and frames the DevAIOps paradigm — explainable, controllable AI agents inside DevOps/DevSecOps (§1, p. 345) — and maps LLM-agent maturity: theme T5 is among the more mature areas while agent explainability (T4) is the least developed (§3, p. 348; §6, p. 351). For agentic systems specifically it synthesizes that tool-using agents outperform non-agent baselines (68% vs 45% top-1 RCA accuracy, with 12-20% accuracy drop when any of the five tools is removed [9], §3.5, p. 349), and it articulates agent-centric gaps: Gap 1, no unified architecture combining pipeline optimization, security and explainability — proposed as an open-source platform with specialized agents for build, security and remediation under one explainability layer (§4.1, p. 349); Gap 3, explainability exists only at model level, not agent level — ReAct traces are unstructured and not auditable, motivating artifact-linked explanations plus SHAP attribution over agent inputs (§4.2, p. 350); Gap 4, LLM hallucination risk in autonomous remediation is unstudied, aligned with the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic AI Applications (2026) issues of autonomous-action violations, cascading agent failures and unauthorized execution (§4.3, p. 350). The trust loop (Fig. 4, p. 350) — explanations feeding OWASP-based validation and risk-tiered human-in-the-loop gating — is a direct architectural prescription for safe agentic remediation.
Limitations / Future Work: Self-reported threats (§5, pp. 350-351): construct validity — keyword/terminological bias despite two-tier terms over five themes; internal validity — single-reviewer screening, only partially mitigated by the deterministic scoring algorithm; external validity — database-coverage bias (Scopus/WoS favored; arXiv-only, non-indexed and grey literature possibly excluded); conclusion validity — quantitative figures taken as reported by original authors, publication bias toward positive findings, and under-representation of 2025-2026 literature. Only 10 of 47 studies received in-depth synthesis due to the conference page limit, and the full 47-study list is available only on request (§2.3, p. 347; §2, p. 346). Future work per gap: an open-source DevAIOps platform with specialized agents under one explainability layer (Gap 1); a multi-dimensional KPI benchmark (MTTR, false fix ratio, test coverage improvement, deployment success rate, security compliance) demonstrated on at least three open-source projects (Gap 2, §4.1, pp. 349-350); a pipeline-native XAI module producing artifact-linked explanations with SHAP attribution (Gap 3, §4.2, p. 350); and measuring hallucination rates of advanced LLMs (GPT-5, Llama 4 Maverick, Mistral Large 3) on real CI/CD failure datasets, with a fix-validation architecture combining static analysis, OWASP Top 10 for LLM and for Agentic AI Applications (2026), and progressive human-in-the-loop gates (Gap 4, §4.3, p. 350).
Relevance to My Thesis: Directly relevant as a secondary foundational map of the thesis terrain (agentic copilot reducing MTTD/MTTR in incident response): it consolidates the LLM-agent incident-management evidence base the thesis builds on ([3][6][8][9], §3.5, p. 349), confirms MTTR as the paradigm's central KPI while exposing the absence of standardized MTTR benchmarks and the non-verifiability of proprietary results (Gap 2, §4.1, pp. 349-350) — which is precisely the evidence-quality problem the thesis's RSL addresses — and its trust loop with risk-tiered human-in-the-loop gating (Fig. 4, p. 350) matches the copilot (human-supervised) posture the thesis defends over full autonomy. Its gap agenda (unified agent architecture, agent-level explainability, hallucination risk) supplies citable motivation for the dissertation's problem statement. Corpus entry: SECONDARY foundational-conditional study under rule R1 (SLR, no primary evidence of its own), with the mandatory stratum caveat — Procedia Computer Science series, A4 stratum (PDR-0006/0007).
Relevance Score: Medium. Thematic alignment is high — LLM agents, auto-remediation, MTTR as explicit KPI and incident-response themes are the review's core — but it contributes secondary evidence only (no own MTTD/MTTR measurement; MTTD never addressed), and it carries the mandatory A4-stratum caveat (Procedia/MobiSPC, PDR-0006/0007), so it supports the thesis's related-work and gap argumentation rather than its empirical base.

Title: Large Language Models for Agentic NetOps and AIOps: Architectures, Evaluation, and Safety (title page, p. 1).
Authors: Muhammad Bilal (School of Computing and Communications, Lancaster University, UK; Senior Member IEEE; corresponding author), Jon Crowcroft (Department of Computer Science and Technology, University of Cambridge, UK; IEEE Fellow), Ruizhi Wang and Xiaolong Xu (School of Software, Nanjing University of Information Science and Technology, China), and Schahram Dustdar (Distributed Systems Group, TU Wien, Austria, and ICREA, Barcelona, Spain; IEEE Fellow) (p. 1, author block and affiliation footnote).
Year & Venue: 2026, arXiv preprint arXiv:2605.12729v2 [cs.NI], version of 15 June 2026 (p. 1, margin stamp). A survey-style journal manuscript not yet published in a peer-reviewed venue at extraction time; the search window itself runs to May 2026 (SS I.C, p. 4).
Core Problem Addressed: LLMs are increasingly used across NetOps and AIOps for incident investigation, root-cause analysis, configuration synthesis and limited self-healing, turning fragmented operational work into a single loop that reads, reasons and acts near live control surfaces (Abstract and SS I, pp. 1-2). This shift collides with growing operational burden (breadth of tool surface, velocity of change, volume of interruption) in SRE organisations that aim to minimise detection and recovery times (SS I, p. 2), yet the field lacks shared terms for autonomy, a stable set of evaluation tasks, and a threat model matching real operational tool surfaces (SS I, p. 2). The survey's core question is how to design, evaluate and govern NetOps/AIOps agents so as to maintain or maximise reliability and security while reducing operational burden, improving outcomes such as diagnostic and mitigation times under explicit safety constraints (SS I.A(d), p. 3). Its central thesis: operational reliability comes not chiefly from the model but from the machinery around it - typed tool interfaces, provenance-aware retrieval, budgets, least privilege, and verification gates at the write boundary (Abstract, p. 1).
Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: Not a new system but a contract-centred taxonomy that treats agentic NetOps/AIOps as constrained operational control (SS I.D, p. 6; Table I, p. 7). Autonomy is modelled as a ladder of four rungs - read-only copilot, tool-grounded analyst, write-limited planner-executor, and closed-loop self-healing controller (Fig. 5, p. 17) - each written as an operational assurance contract C_k = (T_k, R_k, G_k, U_k, B_k) over permitted tools, required evidence, non-bypassable gates, rollout/rollback/audit protocol, and budgets (SS IV.A, Eq. 12, pp. 16-17; Table III, p. 18). Supporting primitives include typed evidence traces E as first-class, scoreable outputs (Eq. 3, pp. 3-4; Eq. 14, p. 17), explicit budgets and stop rules (SS III.A, Eqs. 8-10, pp. 13-14), a non-bypassable 'verification wall' between proposal and execution (SS III.C, Eq. 11, p. 15), a gated planner-executor loop (Algorithm 1, p. 16), and a reviewable human-approval bundle of diff, preconditions, checks, canary plan, rollback triggers and evidence pointers (Eq. 19 and Fig. 6, p. 19). The copilot rung - the thesis-relevant role - is defined as read-only evidence compression and navigation whose success criteria are faster evidence location and fewer missed signals, with bounded tool calls (Pattern A, SS IV.F, p. 20; Table III, p. 18).
Methodology: Secondary study: a structured review protocol with explicit, reproducible scope (SS I.C, pp. 4-5). Searches covered ACM Digital Library, IEEE Xplore, USENIX proceedings, arXiv, Google Scholar, IETF documents, NIST material and selected standards/project pages, mainly for January 2020 - May 2026, with earlier foundational work retained (p. 4). Queries were organised into six strands (NetOps; AIOps/SRE; LLM-agent; evaluation; safety/security; standards/practice) and screened in two stages (title/abstract/venue/keywords, then full text against the survey question) using explicit inclusion and exclusion conditions, deduplication, and preference for peer-reviewed over preprint versions (pp. 4-5). The final coded corpus contains 181 records: 159 peer-reviewed conference or journal papers, 9 preprints and 13 standards, specifications, books, technical reports or official guidance documents (p. 5). Each record was coded along eight dimensions (domain, operational task, autonomy role, tool surface, evidence type, evaluation setting, safety control, contribution type), followed by backward and forward snowballing until saturation of the coding scheme (p. 5). Raw hit counts are deliberately not reported because Google Scholar and standards pages lack stable exportable hit sets (p. 5).
Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: Secondary evidence only - this survey executes no empirical comparison of its own and reports no primary MTTD/MTTR reductions. It treats detection and recovery times as the operational objective ('organizations aim to minimise detection and recovery times', SS I, p. 2; improving 'diagnostic and mitigation times' as the measurable goal, SS I.A(d), p. 3) and, most usefully for this review, operationalises them as workflow-level evaluation metrics: Table VI defines MTTD(proxy) as time from incident start to first correct triage signal or first discriminating query, and MTTR(proxy) as time to verified mitigation in sandbox/replay or time to approved plan in a human-gated setting (SS VII.A, Table VI, p. 32).
