'Improved MTTR with bounded regressions' is set as the success criterion of the closed-loop self-healing rung (Table III, p. 18), and 'time to mitigate' is listed among the operational outcome observables (SS IV.C, p. 19). Secondary evidence cited from primaries: Xpert's LLM query recommendation reduces time-to-signal in a large-scale incident workflow (SS VI.C(a), p. 27), while ITBench reports current agents succeed on only 13.8% of SRE tasks and 25.2% of CISO tasks across 94 scenarios (SS VII.E, p. 34) - which the survey reads as a warning that demonstrated capability does not yet translate into dependable MTTD/MTTR gains.
General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: The survey supplies shared vocabulary and evaluation discipline for the agentic-operations field: the autonomy ladder, assurance contracts, evidence traces, verification wall, budgets and stop rules, positioned explicitly against prior AIOps, LLM4AIOps, network-automation, LLM-agent, RAG and benchmark surveys (SS I.D and Table I, pp. 6-7). It reframes tools as trust boundaries and audit objects rather than mere capability extensions (SS I.D, p. 6; SS II.E(e), pp. 12-13), proposes a five-level evaluation-realism ladder (static QA, tool-use trace replay, sandbox execution, live testbed, canary/rollback-aware evaluation; SS VII.E, pp. 32-34) with a standard report card (Fig. 10, p. 33) and a metrics glossary (Table VI, p. 32), and gives a threat model for agents near control surfaces with a threat-to-control matrix covering prompt injection, RAG poisoning/jamming, telemetry manipulation, excessive agency and exfiltration (Fig. 12, p. 36; Table VII, p. 37). A research agenda recasts open problems as contract-satisfaction questions (Table VIII, p. 42). Multi-agent coordination per se is not the unit of analysis; roles are rungs of a single gated agentic pipeline, with representative systems (DeepLog, Xpert, RCACopilot, RCAgent, TraceRCA, TADBench) mapped onto those rungs (Table IV, p. 30).
Limitations / Future Work: Stated method limits: many operational agent systems are deployed inside companies and described only through engineering reports or not at all, and the LLM-agent literature is changing quickly, so the authors separate stable claims from current observations (SS I.C, p. 5); raw search hit counts are not reported (p. 5); the autonomy-raises-failure-severity design rule is qualitative rather than an empirical measurement (SS IV.E, p. 20). The paper is an arXiv preprint, not yet peer-reviewed (p. 1). The open-problems agenda (SS IX, pp. 39-42; Table VIII, p. 42) lists future work: compositional safety across layers and rollout time, benchmark realism and reproducibility for contract-based evaluation, hybrid causal-LLM operations, security and integrity as contract clauses (confused-deputy tool misuse, injection, poisoning), human factors and accountability, minimal interoperable schemas for tool calls/evidence/diffs/approvals/rollback/audit, and continual operation under drift and cost. The conclusion cautions that public benchmarks rarely capture drift, partial observability, stale documentation, tool failure and adversarial inputs, so claims about closed-loop autonomy should remain modest, while read-only support is already valuable (SS X, p. 43).
Relevance to My Thesis: High-value foundational secondary source for a thesis on an agentic copilot reducing MTTD/MTTR in incident response. It explicitly defines the copilot as the read-only rung of the autonomy ladder, with success criteria of faster evidence location and fewer missed signals under bounded tool budgets (Table III, p. 18; Pattern A, p. 20), and it supplies ready-made, citable operational definitions of MTTD(proxy) and MTTR(proxy) for evaluating such a copilot (Table VI, p. 32), plus the evaluation-realism ladder and report card for designing a defensible measurement protocol (SS VII.E, pp. 32-34; Fig. 10, p. 33). The assurance-contract framing (what the copilot may observe and propose, which gates and audits apply) and the threat model ground the thesis's safety and governance discussion (SS IV.A, pp. 16-17; Table VII, p. 37). Under rule R1 it enters the corpus as a conditional-foundational secondary study: citable for taxonomy, metric definitions, evaluation protocol and safety requirements, but not as primary evidence of MTTD/MTTR effect sizes, since it performs no empirical comparison of its own (SS I.C, pp. 4-5).
Relevance Score: High - the most comprehensive secondary source in the corpus mapping Agentic AI onto NetOps/AIOps incident workflows, with an explicit copilot-rung definition and operational MTTD/MTTR proxy metrics directly reusable by the thesis (Table III, p. 18; Table VI, p. 32). Scored as foundational-conditional because it is a preprint survey of 181 records with no primary empirical MTTD/MTTR evidence of its own (p. 1; SS I.C, p. 5).

Title: Advancing Autonomous Incident Response: Leveraging LLMs and Cyber Threat Intelligence (title page, p. 1).
Authors: Amine Tellache (OODRIVE - Trusted Cloud Solutions, Paris, and L3i Lab, University of La Rochelle), Abdelaziz Amara Korba (L3i Lab, University of La Rochelle, and German University of Technology in Oman - GUtech), Amdjed Mokhtari and Horea Moldovan (both OODRIVE), and Yacine Ghamri-Doudane (L3i Lab, University of La Rochelle) (p. 1) — an industry-academic collaboration, with the system evaluated on the vendor's own enterprise SIEM alerts (§III.A, p. 4).
Year & Venue: 2025, GLOBECOM 2025 — IEEE Global Communications Conference, Communication & Information Systems Security track, proceedings pp. 25-30, DOI 10.1109/GLOBECOM59602.2025.11432623 (p. 1, footer).
Core Problem Addressed: Security teams performing incident response are overwhelmed by alert fatigue and high false-positive rates: SOC analysts face an average of 4,484 alerts per day and spend nearly three hours daily on manual triage (§I, p. 1, citing [2]). Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI) could enrich and contextualize these alerts, but CTI is vast, heterogeneous, unstructured and fragmented across diverse sources, so searching, reading and correlating reports demands additional manual effort, highly skilled personnel and costly tooling, and is too slow for real-time attacks (Abstract, p. 1; §I, p. 1). Multi-cloud environments add fragmented security models, and generic IR playbooks lack actionable guidance for less experienced teams (§I, p. 1). Existing LLM uses in CTI remain largely passive (summarization, TTP mapping), with a limited role in active incident response, while fine-tuning LLMs for continuously evolving CTI is costly (§I, p. 2).
Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: A Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)-based incident response framework that automates the workflows of SOC analysts, CTI analysts and incident responders (§II.A, p. 2; Fig. 1, p. 3). It takes a SIEM alert as input and runs two phases: (1) a hybrid Retrieval phase combining a standard search — an IOC Parser extracts domains, hashes, IPs and URLs, then queries private CTI platform APIs (VirusTotal in the experiments) for reputation, geolocation and historical malicious activity (§II.C, p. 3) — with an NLP similarity search over a Chroma vector database of embedded APT/cybercrime campaign reports from VX Underground, using an LLM-generated 'augmented alert' as the query and cosine similarity for matching (§II.B-II.C, p. 3; Eq. 1, p. 4; §III.A, p. 4); (2) an Augmented Generation phase in which a pre-trained LLM (GPT-4o) receives a structured prompt with the alert plus concatenated retrieved contexts and generates an incident response plan (§II.D, p. 4; Fig. 1b, p. 3). Agency is limited: the system is a single-LLM, single-pass RAG pipeline with tool-style API retrieval that produces a textual mitigation strategy for human responders — there is no autonomous execution of actions, no multi-step planning loop, no self-correction and no multi-agent orchestration (the only multi-LLM element is the evaluation ensemble, §III.B, pp. 4-5). The 'autonomous security operations' of the title is framed as a direction this work lays a foundation for (Abstract, p. 1), making it an advisory copilot for IR teams rather than an agentic responder. New CTI is integrated by re-embedding reports, avoiding fine-tuning (§II.A, pp. 2-3).
Methodology: Design-and-evaluate study on two alert datasets (§III.A, p. 4): 100 real-world alerts randomly selected from the authors' company LogPoint SIEM between August 10 and September 8, 2024, and 10 simulated alerts generated in a controlled Proxmox test environment with an ELK-stack SIEM, Elastic Defend agents on Windows and Linux victim VMs, and MITRE Caldera emulating APT adversaries with ATT&CK TTPs (e.g., Automated Collection T1119, Exfiltration Over C2 Channel T1041, Process Discovery T1057, Process Injection T1055.002) (Fig. 2, p. 4). Evaluation uses a dual paradigm (§III.B, pp. 4-5): automated LLM-as-judge scoring on a 1-5 scale for three RAG metrics — Answer Relevance, Context Relevance and Groundedness — by three open models (Mistral-large-2407, Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct), each prompted to score and justify, cross-validated by a manual assessment from one in-house cybersecurity expert on the 10 simulated alerts (Table III, p. 6). There is no baseline condition (no comparison against unassisted analysts or another tool) and no time-to-respond measurement; all outcomes are response-quality scores (§III.C, pp. 5-6).
Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: Not specified quantitatively — the paper measures no detection or response times and executes no empirical comparison against a concrete baseline (human analysts or an alternative system), so no comparative MTTD/MTTR benefit can be asserted (Art. I). The Abstract's claims of 'alleviating analyst workload and reducing response latency' (p. 1) are motivational, not measured. What is actually measured are LLM-judged quality scores on a 1-5 scale (§III.C, pp. 5-6): on 100 real-world alerts, Answer Relevance averages near 5 (e.g., 4.97 Mistral-large, 4.95 Llama-3.1-70B), Groundedness exceeds 4 (4.53, 4.19, 4.51), but Context Relevance is low at ~3.15-3.62 (Table I, p. 5), attributed to false-positive alerts and IOCs absent from VirusTotal; on 10 simulated (all true-positive) alerts, Context Relevance improves to ~4.0-4.55 (Table II, p. 5); the single-expert manual evaluation gives 4.20 Answer Relevance, 4.10 Context Relevance and 4.10 Groundedness (Table III, p. 6). These quality scores are the only empirical evidence; any MTTD/MTTR effect remains hypothetical.
General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: Contribution to the agentic agenda is deliberate but modest: the paper argues for moving LLMs in CTI from passive tasks (summarization, TTP mapping) to active incident response (§I, p. 2) and demonstrates a reusable pattern — hybrid retrieval that fuses structured tool calls to CTI platform APIs with semantic search over an embedded CTI corpus, feeding a generation prompt (§II.C-II.D, pp. 3-4) — plus a fine-tuning-free adaptation strategy (continuous re-embedding of new CTI; §II.A, pp. 2-3). Its dual evaluation paradigm, using an ensemble of three LLM judges cross-validated by human experts, with the stated intent of later using automated scores as a filter to retain only accurate responses (§III.C.2, p. 5), is a transferable quality-gate design for agentic pipelines. However, the system itself exhibits limited agency — one retrieval-generation pass, no action execution, no inter-agent coordination — so it informs the perception/enrichment and advisory layers of future agentic IR systems rather than demonstrating autonomy; the authors position it as 'establishing a foundation for intelligent, adaptive cybersecurity frameworks' (Abstract, p. 1).
Limitations / Future Work: Acknowledged limitations: low Context Relevance on real-world alerts caused by false positives, IOCs not recognized in VirusTotal and CTI reports lacking detail on specific campaigns (§III.C.1, p. 5; §III.C.3, p. 6) — in those cases the system generates coherent output not grounded in retrieved context (§III.C.3, p. 6). Reviewer-noted gaps: no baseline comparison and no time/latency measurement despite the response-latency claim in the Abstract; only 10 simulated alerts and a single in-house expert validator (Table III, p. 6); LLM-as-judge scores from only three models with varying sensitivity (Table I, p. 5); GPT-4o selection justified by a leaderboard rather than task-specific comparison (§III.A, p. 4); vendor-internal alert data limits reproducibility. Future work (§III.C.1, p. 5; §IV, p. 6): add trusted private databases such as CrowdStrike and broader CTI report coverage; integrate the knowledge base with the OpenCTI platform (§II.B, p. 3); extend outputs to a wider range of cybersecurity roles and enhance model reasoning; and harden the system against adversarial attacks.
Relevance to My Thesis: Partially on-construct: the paper targets the thesis domain (incident response in SOC operations) and the copilot intent — an LLM assistant that enriches alerts with CTI and drafts actionable response plans to relieve analyst workload (Abstract, p. 1; §II.A, p. 2) — and its hybrid RAG retrieval and LLM-judge-plus-expert evaluation design are directly reusable in the thesis's enrichment and quality-gate layers. However, it provides no MTTD/MTTR evidence (no baseline, no time metrics; §III, pp. 4-6) and exhibits limited agency: a single-pass advisory RAG pipeline without autonomous action, planning loops or multi-agent coordination (§II, pp. 2-4), so it supports the thesis's motivation and architecture chapters rather than its effectiveness claims. It enters the corpus with the mandatory stratum caveat — the IEEE GLOBECOM conference series is an A4-stratum venue, so inclusion carries the qualification formalized in PDR-0006/0007 — and with the limited-agency caveat recorded in the cycle evaluation.
Relevance Score: Medium — strong domain and copilot-intent match (CTI-grounded LLM assistant generating IR plans from SIEM alerts) with a reusable hybrid-RAG and dual-evaluation design, but it measures only LLM-judged response quality (Tables I-III, pp. 5-6), offers no MTTD/MTTR or baseline evidence, and the solution's agency is limited to single-pass advisory generation; the A4-stratum caveat (PDR-0006/0007) applies.

Title: Large Language Models for Security Operations Centers: A Comprehensive Survey (title page, p. 1). Review article (open access), presented by the authors as "the first comprehensive and structured analysis of LLM integration into SOC operations" (Abstract, p. 1).
Authors: Ali Habibzadeh, Farid Feyzi (corresponding author) and Reza Ebrahimi Atani, all with the Faculty of Engineering, University of Guilan, Rasht, Guilan, Iran (p. 1) — an academic-authored secondary study with no industry affiliation and no funding received (Funding statement, p. 28).
Year & Venue: 2026, Journal of Electrical and Computer Engineering (Wiley, open access), vol. 2026, article ID 3383674, DOI 10.1155/jece/3383674; received 14 December 2025, revised 25 April 2026, accepted 18 May 2026 (p. 1). A preprint was previously published on arXiv (2509.10858) (Disclosure, p. 28). Venue stratum caveat: Qualis A3 (PDR-0007).
Core Problem Addressed: SOCs face escalating operational strain — alert fatigue, excessive false positives and a critical skills gap — leading to delayed detections and delayed incident response (Abstract, p. 1; §1, p. 1): the SANS 2025 SOC survey identifies lack of skilled staff as the primary operational challenge (§1, p. 1), the Ponemon Institute reports an average of 258 days to identify and contain a breach (§1, p. 1), and Tier-1 analyst burnout and turnover increase the mean time to resolution for critical events (§2.2, p. 3). At the same time, the literature on LLMs in cybersecurity is fragmented: prior surveys are either too broad (security/privacy), too narrow (single tasks such as vulnerability detection), or pre-LLM SOC studies published before 2021, leaving no structured, operationally focused analysis of LLM integration across the distinct phases of SOC workflows (§2.4, p. 4; Table 2, p. 6).
Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: A SECONDARY STUDY — no new system is built. The survey contributes (i) a foundational overview of SOC operations, analyst Tiers 1-4 and challenges (§2.2, pp. 3-4; Figure 2, p. 4); (ii) a dual-framework structured analysis mapping LLM applications across the SOC Detection/Analysis/Response phases to the NIST CSF functions, with MITRE ATT&CK as a granular lens for detection capabilities (§2.3, p. 4; Table 1, p. 5); and (iii) a research roadmap (§8, pp. 25-28). Agentic AI appears as one of five adaptation methods (pretraining, fine-tuning, prompt engineering, RAG, agents — §2.1, pp. 2-3) and is the dominant pattern in the Response phase: LLM-based agents/multi-agent systems are highly adopted in incident response (Table 14, p. 25), e.g., Audit-LLM's multiagent debate for insider-threat detection (§5.1, p. 8), IDS-Agent (Table 4, p. 10), RCACopilot deployed at Microsoft, RCAgent and Flow-of-Action for root cause analysis (§6.5, pp. 20-21; Table 12, p. 22), and Nissist, AutoBnB and IRCopilot for incident mitigation/response (§7.2, pp. 24-25). Maturity per task is assessed with a consolidated 4-stage TRL scale (§3.1, pp. 5-6).
Methodology: Systematic literature review explicitly following Kitchenham's SLR guidelines (planning, conducting, reporting) (§3, p. 4). Five research questions (RQ1 LLMs used; RQ2-RQ4 adaptation per SOC phase; RQ5 challenges/future directions) (§3.1, p. 5). Search in five databases — ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, arXiv — supplemented by Google Scholar, with a declared Boolean search string combining LLM terms and SOC/cybersecurity terms (§3.2, p. 6). Inclusion: papers 2021-2025 that directly employ LLMs in their architecture with a SOC-aligned downstream task; exclusion: duplicates, non-English, non-full-length papers (books, short papers, tutorials); screening by title/abstract/conclusion with full-text review when ambiguous (§3.3, p. 6). Final corpus: 216 studies, whose per-year/per-phase distribution shows a sharp increase and a clear decline in volume from Detection to Response (§3.4, p. 6; Figure 3, p. 7). Maturity is assessed via the NASA/ISO 16290 TRL framework consolidated into four stages (§3.1, pp. 5-6). The paper reports no PRISMA flow diagram, no inter-rater reliability statistics and no formal quality appraisal of primary studies.
Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: Secondary evidence only — the survey runs no empirical comparison of its own and reports no MTTD/MTTR measurements; all figures below are relayed from referenced primary studies. (1) Nissist [272] (LLM multi-agent incident mitigation at enterprise cloud scale): time-to-mitigate reduction of 98.93% for simple incidents and 94.85% for hard ones versus manual mitigation, with 77.19% / 52.63% full-automation success rates (§7.2, pp. 24-25). (2) AdaptiveLog [252]: ~73% average reduction in LLM-related costs across six log-analysis tasks — efficiency, not a time metric (§6.5, pp. 21-22). (3) Motivational context, not results: Ponemon's 258 days to identify and contain a breach (§1, p. 1) and burnout-driven increases in mean time to resolution (§2.2, p. 3). MTTR appears explicitly only as a recommended future measurement: SOC engineers should pilot agent-based RAG for alert enrichment and "measure the reduction in mean time to respond (MTTR)" before broadening deployment (§8.2, p. 27). No MTTD figures appear anywhere in the paper.
General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: The survey positions agents as the architectural answer to the hardest SOC tasks while flagging their cost: agent-based systems incur higher computational overhead from iterative reasoning, multiple model calls and tool interactions (§2.1, p. 3). For root cause analysis, LLM-based agents are deemed the more suitable choice because they can interact with external environments, synthesize high-volume multisource data, adapt without retraining and explain their outputs (§6.5, p. 20). In incident response, multiagent architectures mimic human IR team structures with specialized collaborative components, mitigating factual inaccuracy and context loss common in monolithic LLMs, and are called "a transformative approach for more efficient and effective IR" (§7.2, p. 25; Table 14, p. 25). Named agentic exemplars include Audit-LLM (pairwise evidence-based multiagent debate, §5.1, p. 8), RCAgent with observation-snapshot-key context compression validated on Alibaba Cloud (§6.5, p. 21) and AutoBnB simulating IR team structures (§7.2, p. 24; Table 14, p. 25). Future directions push the field toward agent-based RAG, autonomous security decision-making under human supervision, and formal human-in-the-loop (HITL) protocols with escalation paths and override-feedback registries (§8.2, pp. 26-27); the reference list includes dedicated Agentic AI literature (refs. [289-290], p. 38).
Limitations / Future Work: Challenges catalogued for LLMs in SOCs (§8.1, pp. 25-26): resource intensity and financial barriers; hallucination and bias (fabricated threat indicators, false-positive escalations); black-box opacity and catastrophic forgetting; attack-surface expansion (prompt injection, data poisoning, model inversion); a data trilemma (availability, relevance/concept drift, text-vs-nonlinguistic structure mismatch); integration with heterogeneous SOC stacks lacking standardized APIs; regulatory compliance (GDPR/HIPAA vs. opaque commercial APIs); and balancing human expertise with automation. Research gaps: coverage is heavily concentrated on NIST "Detect", with significant gaps in "Protect" and especially "Recover" (Table 1, p. 5; §8.2, pp. 27-28; §9, p. 28), and the Response phase is the least researched due to operational risk, scarce real-world datasets and missing IR benchmarks (§3.4, p. 6; §7.2, p. 25). Future directions (§8.2, pp. 26-28): XAI for SOC trust, LLM+federated learning, robust benchmarks and SOC simulation environments, agent-based RAG, autonomous decision-making with phased low-risk rollout, hybrid rule-based/ML/LLM architectures, HITL protocols, and filling the Protect/Recover gaps. As a survey, it also carries methodological limitations it does not discuss: no quality appraisal, no inter-rater statistics and no PRISMA reporting (§3, pp. 4-6).
Relevance to My Thesis: Directly relevant as domain-mapping foundation: it is the first structured survey of exactly the environment where my proposed agentic copilot operates (LLMs across SOC detection, analysis and incident response), and it independently corroborates the thesis problem framing — skills gap, alert fatigue and delayed response quantified via SANS 2025 and Ponemon's 258-day containment window (§1, p. 1). It supplies reusable scaffolding (NIST CSF x MITRE ATT&CK mapping, Table 1, p. 5; 4-stage TRL maturity, §3.1, pp. 5-6), a catalogue of agentic IR systems to position the copilot against (Nissist, AutoBnB, IRCopilot — Table 14, p. 25), secondary MTTR-adjacent evidence (Nissist's 94.85-98.93% time-to-mitigate reduction, §7.2, pp. 24-25), and an explicit research-gap argument the thesis exploits: Response is the least-studied phase and agent-based RAG pilots should be evaluated by MTTR reduction (§8.2, p. 27). Corpus status: enters as a foundational-conditional SECONDARY study under rule R1 — usable for background, taxonomy and gap justification, not as primary MTTD/MTTR evidence — with the mandatory stratum caveat: venue is Qualis A3 (PDR-0007).
Relevance Score: Medium — High thematic overlap (LLM/agentic systems for SOC incident response, with explicit MTTR framing and a Response-phase gap the thesis addresses), but it is a secondary study with no primary MTTD/MTTR evidence of its own, published in a Qualis A3 venue, so it serves as foundational context and gap justification rather than core empirical evidence (R1; PDR-0007).

Title: An adaptive agentic AI framework for counterfactual validation and adversarial lookahead in automated incident response (title page, p. 1). The proposed framework is named CIPHER-A — Counterfactual Incident Response Planning with Hallucination-Aware Evaluation and Reasoning — Adaptive (Abstract, p. 1).
Authors: Sheetal Prasad Kizhakel (School of Computer Science and Engineering, Vellore Institute of Technology, Vellore, Tamil Nadu, India) and Sagar Dhanraj Pande (Department of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning, Symbiosis Institute of Technology, Pune Campus, Symbiosis International (Deemed University), Pune, India; corresponding author) (p. 1).
Year & Venue: 2026, Discover Artificial Intelligence (Springer Nature), vol. 6, article 970, DOI 10.1007/s44163-026-02058-6, Open Access under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (p. 1); received 13 April 2026, accepted 13 August 2026 (p. 26).
Core Problem Addressed: Industrial SOAR platforms (Palo Alto Cortex XSOAR, Splunk SOAR, IBM QRadar) respond via pre-coded playbooks and cannot generalize to dynamic multi-stage APT attacks (§1, p. 2), while current LLM-integrated tools (Microsoft Security Copilot, Google Chronicle AI) generate a response plan once at alert ingestion and execute it sequentially, applying LLM solutions without considering the danger those actions pose to live systems and treating threats as static attacks rather than dynamic adversarial processes — 'blind execution' (Abstract, p. 1; §1, p. 2). A systematic comparison of 25 works from 2022-2026 (Table 1, pp. 4-5) identifies three unaddressed gaps: (i) no pre-execution counterfactual validation of response actions, (ii) no post-execution adversarial state update closing the loop on the remaining plan, and (iii) no dynamic attacker model of adaptation between response steps (§2.2, pp. 7-8).
Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: CIPHER-A, an agentic AI closed-loop pipeline of five components (Table 3, p. 15) orchestrated as a LangGraph v0.2 typed state graph with conditional routing (§4.5, p. 13): AISNA normalizes Wazuh 4.7 SIEM alerts into the incident state tuple s=(A,N,U,T,Psi) (§4.5, pp. 12-13); the Counterfactual Validation Engine (CVE, Claude 3 Sonnet API) generates K=3 LLM outcome scenarios per proposed action and computes a Risk Score and a Composite Validation Score CVS = alpha*RS + beta*C (asset criticality) + gamma*U (urgency) (Eqs. 1-3, p. 10), routing each action to EXECUTE / MODIFY / ESCALATE against calibrated thresholds tau_low=0.35 and tau_high=0.65 before any live system change (Eq. 4, §4.2, p. 11); the Attacker Simulation Agent (ASA, Mistral-7B-Instruct deployed locally) predicts the adversary state transition after each executed action, grounded in MITRE ATT&CK v14.1 (14 tactics, 190+ techniques), and feeds the updated threat state into the next validation cycle (§4.3, p. 11); the Execution Dispatcher executes validated actions via live CrowdStrike Falcon API v2.0, AWS IAM/EC2 and Microsoft Active Directory LDAP APIs; and the Audit & Re-validation Controller persists every step to PostgreSQL 16 and triggers replanning when the running RPDR exceeds 0.30 (§4.5, p. 13; Table 3, p. 15). The agentic role is autonomous validated execution with calibrated human-in-the-loop escalation (ESCALATE suspends the graph and notifies an analyst, §4.5, p. 13), i.e., a safety-gated autonomous responder rather than a purely advisory copilot.
Methodology: Framework construction plus controlled quantitative evaluation of a Python 3.11 prototype on a single NVIDIA A100 80GB host (§4.6, p. 15). Three public datasets (Table 2, p. 9): DARPA OPTC as primary (143 incident traces, 3 APT scenarios — lateral movement, privilege escalation + exfiltration, C2 + ransomware — across 500+ enterprise hosts; §5, p. 16), MITRE ATT&CK v14.1 as adversarial knowledge base, and CTU-13 for collateral-damage validation (847 blocking tests, §5.3, p. 20). Six system configurations analyze the identical 143 alerts through the identical Wazuh 4.7 ingestion pipeline, 'creating a controlled environment for the experiment' (§5, p. 16): three internal baselines executed by the authors in one unified environment — Baseline SOAR (rule-based, no LLM), LLM-SOAR (no pre-execution validation) and CIPHER-static (CVE-only ablation) (§5.4, p. 22) — plus two external adaptive baselines, Liu [10] (MA-LLM-IR) and Babar et al. [23] (HRL-CIDR), whose RPDR/FSR/EA/MTTC values were NOT originally reported by those authors but were derived by the present authors applying CIPHER-A's scoring framework to each paper's published performance indicators, explicitly flagged as 'indicative rather than directly comparable' and 'not independently replicable' (§5.1, p. 17; §5.4, pp. 21-23). Metrics: the new RPDR (Eq. 6, p. 12), cross-validated at 97.2% agreement against DARPA OPTC red-team ground-truth pivot logs (§4.4, p. 12), False Safety Rate (FSR), Escalation Accuracy (EA) and MTTC; Wilcoxon signed-rank tests on n=143 incidents (Table 8, p. 20); weights/thresholds calibrated by grid search on an OPTC validation split of n=92 (§4.1, p. 10; §4.2, p. 11) with one-at-a-time sensitivity analysis (§5.5, pp. 23-24).
Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: The paper reports neither MTTD nor MTTR by name: detection is delegated to the Wazuh SIEM (MTTD out of scope), and the time metric is MTTC — mean time to contain, from alert ingestion to full containment, in minutes (Table 7 note, §5.2, p. 18) — a containment-side proxy for MTTR. CIPHER-A reduces MTTC from 14.3 ± 2.1 min (Baseline SOAR) to 8.9 ± 1.4 min, a 37.8% reduction (Table 5, p. 16; Table 7, p. 19; Fig. 6, p. 20; Abstract, p. 1); this baseline is an author-implemented rule-based playbook system executed on the same 143 OPTC alerts in the same environment, i.e., an executed internal comparison (§5, p. 16; §5.4, p. 22). Decomposition: 2.1 min automated pipeline (7.2 actions x 2.45 s) plus 6.8 min analyst review on the 8.3% escalated actions, versus 14.3 min with 100% manual review in Baseline SOAR (Table 5, p. 16). Ablation: adding the CVE alone cuts MTTC from 11.8 (LLM-SOAR) to 10.2 min (-13.6% relative); adding the ASA cuts it further to 8.9 min (-12.7% relative) (§5.2, p. 19). Against the external indicative baselines, CIPHER-A's 8.9 min compares with 12.6 ± 1.8 min derived for Liu [10] and 11.1 ± 1.7 min derived for Babar et al. [23] (a 19.8% MTTC improvement) — figures computed by the present authors from those papers' published indicators, not reported by the original works (§5.4, p. 22; Table 7, p. 19). Wilcoxon MTTC tests versus the three internal baselines are all significant at p < 0.001 (Table 8, p. 20). Supporting safety/quality results: mean RPDR 15.6% vs 64.4% (Baseline SOAR) and 38.2% (CIPHER-static; 59.2% relative reduction), FSR 3.2% vs 22.7% baseline (a sevenfold reduction, §6, p. 25), EA 91.7% (Tables 6-7, pp. 17 and 19).
General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: Claims three firsts for agentic security automation: the first pre-execution consequence-prediction mechanism for individual IR actions (CVE), the first use of MITRE ATT&CK as a grounding constraint for real-time adversarial state prediction inside an active IR pipeline (ASA), and RPDR as the first quantitative metric operationalizing the necessity of adaptive sequential re-validation (§1.1, pp. 3-6). Demonstrates a heterogeneous two-LLM agent design — cloud Claude 3 Sonnet for validation reasoning plus local Mistral-7B for low-latency adversary simulation — wired as LangGraph conditional nodes, with quantified operating cost (~700 tokens and 2.45 s per action; mean 8,330 tokens per incident; Tables 4-5, pp. 15-16). The ablation shows complementary agent roles: the CVE contributes the larger share of the FSR reduction (61.2%) while the ASA feedback loop contributes the larger share of the RPDR reduction (56.4%) (§5.2, pp. 19-20). ASA attacker-adaptation prediction reaches 78.6-84.1% accuracy per scenario and the CVE attains 94.3% collateral-damage prediction accuracy on 847 CTU-13 blocking tests (95% CI [92.5, 95.6]) (§5.3, pp. 20-21; Fig. 7, p. 21). The paper also delineates itself from the concurrent AgentSOC [24]: defender-action counterfactuals with live execution APIs versus attacker-path counterfactuals in dry-run mode (§2.1, p. 7).
Limitations / Future Work: The external baseline comparisons (Liu [10], Babar et al. [23]) are indicative cross-framework estimates computed by the present authors and 'cannot serve as independently replicable evaluations' (§5.4, pp. 22-23); the CVE/ASA ablation attribution is incremental within a fixed sequence, not an interaction-free causal estimate (§5.2, pp. 19-20). A residual 15.6% RPDR persists where ASA prediction confidence fell below the 0.7 update threshold (§5.1, p. 18). The prototype ran on a single A100 host without concurrent-incident stress testing; Claude API rate limits, single-GPU Mistral-7B capacity, execution-API quotas, PostgreSQL contention and analyst availability are expected bottlenecks, and the authors warn the 8.9-minute MTTC 'should not be extrapolated' to larger or highly concurrent environments until load tests are performed (§5.6, pp. 24-25). The first-hop-only subgraph fallback for highly connected hosts may omit second-hop dependencies and reduce collateral-damage accuracy (§4.2, p. 11; §5.6, p. 24), and DARPA OPTC is a controlled APT simulation with weights calibrated on a single n=92 split (§4.1, p. 10). Future work: knowledge-graph encodings of topology for blast-radius analysis, federated CIPHER-A sharing ASA forecasts across organizations, and formal causal models replacing probabilistic LLM estimates (§7, p. 25). The authors used GPT-4 to improve language clarity (Declarations, p. 26).
Relevance to My Thesis: High relevance: this is one of the four primary studies in the nominal-times cluster reporting response-time metrics against a baseline. It provides an executed, controlled empirical comparison — six configurations over the identical 143 DARPA OPTC alerts and ingestion pipeline (§5, p. 16) — in which an agentic pipeline with human-in-the-loop escalation reduces MTTC from 14.3 to 8.9 min (-37.8%, Table 5, p. 16; Table 7, p. 19) with Wilcoxon p < 0.001 (Table 8, p. 20), satisfying Art. I for the containment-time claim against the concrete internal Baseline SOAR. It directly evidences the thesis mechanism: safety-gated agentic validation plus selective escalation (8.3% of actions, 91.7% accuracy) removes the human-review bottleneck that dominates containment time, i.e., the MTTR side of the thesis; MTTD is not addressed since detection is delegated to the SIEM (§5.2, p. 18). Mandatory caveats: the venue (Discover Artificial Intelligence) is Qualis A3, below the review's A1-A2 preferred threshold, so the study enters under the stratum waiver PDR-0007; and all figures attributed to the external baselines Liu [10] and Babar et al. [23] are author-derived indicative estimates (§5.4, pp. 21-23), so only the internal comparisons (Baseline SOAR, LLM-SOAR, CIPHER-static) count as executed empirical evidence under Art. I.
Relevance Score: High — it delivers an executed baseline comparison with nominal containment-time numbers (MTTC 14.3 -> 8.9 min, -37.8%, p < 0.001) on a public enterprise-scale APT dataset, with an agentic human-in-the-loop architecture squarely in the thesis scope. The Qualis A3 stratum (PDR-0007) and the indicative nature of the external baselines temper, but do not negate, its evidentiary weight.
